To constitute a truly happy home, there should be pretty little personal adornments on the part of the wife who thereby showsp. desire torplease her husband and to :dal the general attractions of her home. A pleasant word on her part, when the overworked man cornea home, often eats away the raw edge of the trouble on his mind, and draws out a corresponding desire tO be both agreeable and respectful, which characteristics are always accompanied by affection. If Cheerfulness and amiability are not cultivated, rudeness, roughness, and impatience will soon be followed by inso- lence ; and when sweet temper gives way to anger and dis- cord, the home circle is no longPr attractive, and is almost certain to be shunned. BIRDS AND THE COLD WEATTIEIL—Never within the recollection of the oldest boy going have the "feathered tribes," as our poetic grandfathers used to, say, shown such signs of feeling the cold. Sea-gulls at London Bridge in severe frosts are well within living memory; built is not usual figardens within the fOur-mile-raditis- from Char-fife Cross to see thrushes; greenfinches, and robins in considerable liunibers. A solitary thrush or other songster is not uncom- mon, but this winter the strange birds have come right up to the windows and doom, by threes and fours, in search ot food. The cats have had a tine luxurious time of it. They were at first very much puzzled by the snow-whirlwind, but. they soon found out that the sparrows were half palsied With cold, and made prime bags of that sort of game.—From the Boys' Newpaper. Tim Tatra MAN.—Mind is superior to things, not because it is superior to law, but because it is a law unto itself. The true man is he who freely and gladly obeys the law of his being, who is not drawn hither and thither by every passing impulse or influence, but steadfastly follows the leadings of his conscience and his own ever progressing standard of right doing. Thus he is, first of all, true to himself, anet in so being, he is true to all others. If he makes a promise, he is sure to keep it; if he enters into a contract, he will fulfil it both in letter and in spirit; if he assumes a relation, he will be certain to discharge its obligations—and this not from outward compulsion, not from the fear of social or personal disfavour, not from the influence of circumstances or feelings, bat froth his own secret loyalty to the right, which is the essence of all true freedom,. While the tele- phone creates its own-- earrent ot-eleetricitAii cifitain pro- portion of the Working force which moy.es Mb disc of the transmitting instrument being -Impended in this operation, Microphone takes a current already provided by a battery, and merely varies the amount of the current passing from one ththe uthermf its opposing-contact:mfanes;--whole of the maive force therefore, generally speaking,' ii ex- pended in varying the resistance. -With this great saving, the instrument is much more susceptible to very slight sounds, but it is also fatally Susceptible. to the influence of very alight mechanical movements which vary the relations of the contact surfaces to each other, thereby varying the amount of current passing, and producing corresponding sounds In the' telephone. These sounds are usually very loud and sharp, and interfere materially with the 'hearing as well as with the transmission of regular musical tones. It may be briefly put that for the delicate purpose in question the telephone transmitstocr little, .and the microphone, in any of -its present forms, transmits too much. Bevetal microphones and sphygmophones for auscultation have been , constructed in France and , Germany. _ pr. Blake says that ' he has had no opportunity to experiment with them, but from the details of their construction -they, do not differ essentially from those used in these experiments,-and )he is disposed to judge them to be °pent° the Sarne'objectitns.- .British Medical Journal.' \ , SPEED AT WHICH WINOS ARE DRIVEN.—The speed at which some wings are driven is enornaous. It is occasionally so great as to cause the.pinions to emit a drumming sonind. To this source the buzz of. the fly, the drone of the bee, and the boom of the beetle are to- be referred. When a grouse, partridge, or pheasant suddenly springs-into the air the sound produced by the whirring of its -wings greatly, re- ., sembles that produced by the contact of teel with the ra- idly revolving stone of the knife-grinder. It has been estimated that the common fly moves its wings 330 times per second, I.e, -19,800 times per minute; and that the but- terfly moves* wings nine-times per second, or 540 times per minute. These movements represent an incredibly high speed even at the Mote- orthe _wings, but the speed is enor- mously increased at the tips:of the wings, from the fact al- ready pointed out, that the ;tips rotate upon the roots as centres. In reality, and as has been already indicated, the -speed of the tips of the wings increases in proportion as the tips are removed from the axes of rotation and in proportion as the wings are long. This is explained on a principle well understood in mechanics. If a rod or wing hinged at one point be made to vibrate, the free end of the rod or wing always passes through a very much greater space in a given time than the part nearer the root of the wing. The pro- gressive increase in the speed of the wings, in proportion as the wings become larger, explains why the wings of bats and birds are not driven at the extravagant speed of insect wings, and how the large and long wings of large bats and birds are driven more leisurely than the small and short wings • of- small bats -and birds. That the wing is driven more slowly in proportion to its length-is proved by experi- ment, and by observing the flight of large and small birds of the same genus. Thus large gulls flap their wings much more slowly than small gulls, the configuration and relatif-. size of theswings to the body being the same in both. .Thist is a hopeful feature in the construction of- flying machines, as there can be no doubt that comparatively very slow movements will suffice for driving the long powerful wings , required to elevate and propel flying machines. . The speed of the wing is in part regulated by the amplitude of the wing.: Thus if the wing be broad as well as long. the bents are necessarily reduced in frequency. This is especially; true of the heron, which is one of the most picturesque and at the same time one of the slowest flying birds We have: I have timed the heron on several occasions, and find that in ordinary flights its wings make exactly sixty up and sixty down strokeas i.e., 120 beats a minute. In the pterodactyl, 'the great extinct Saurian, the wing was enormously,elon- gated, and in this particular instance probably-from frfty to sixty beats of the wing per minute sufficed for flight. Fifty or sixty pulsations of the wing perminute do hot involve much Wear and tear of the working parts, and I am strongly of:opinioti that artificial flight, if once Achieved, will bes. come a comparatively safe means of locomotion as far as the machinery required is concerned. It is quite evident, judg- ing from what we find 'in nature, that flight is to a large ex- tent a question of weight and-prer of body and size and speed of 'wing.-,,Frcren4s Alapciezan• :,-...

Lechmere, viz., the butler, the head gamekeeper, and an engineer,'were drowned in the Severn on Monday, while returning from Tipton in the ,yacht's small boat. - , The arrivals of live stock and fresh meat at Liverpool from the United States and Canada last week were as follows 627 cattle, 229 sheep, 5,394 -quarters Of beef, 956 carcases of mutton, and 944 dead rtigs. A housekeeper to a gentleman residing at Gravesend hag been murdered, and tha crime is supposed to have been per- petrated by a'soldier in the 52nd Light Infantry,"stationed at Chatham; who is-in custody. A woman has died at the Walton Workhouse, aged 104 years. She was a native ef Ireland, aiad has been in the workhouse-einee-1800. She was constantly visited by a lady aged seventy, to whom, in her early years, she was nurse. The Daily 'New gave prominence,'on Saturday, to a re- port that a plbt to blow up Windsor Castle had been dis- covered, and that the return of the Court from Osborne had in consequence been postponed. Despatches from Windsor state that nothing is known there of .the-" plot." • A quarterly statement as to pauperism, lust Issued, shows the number of paupers in receipt of 'relief on the last dast,' of the hit week of the' quarters ended Christmas 1878, f 879,0 and 1880. The paupers in 1880, as compared with those of 1879, decreased 43,320,--or 5-5 per cent. ;Iphut as -conl pa'red.with 1878 there was an increase of 9,631, or 130 per , cent.-- - • On Sunday night, Mary Payne, a womanFlipwards` of 30 years of age, was-- mardeted ly ben husband William Payntt, nut and bolt maker, Darlaston, South aaffordshiro,- The man had been; heard to threaten his Wife, and accomplished his design by cutting her throat front ear to ear, afterwards _throwing the knife :behind' the . • <,=,- • re. On Monday, David Cottle and William Risdon were arrested at Glasgow, on a charge of forgery. They had in their possession 4346. Cottle, on being asked how he came , by the money, replied that he was in the employment of a rm of writers in Bristol, and on Saturday last otataining,a, cheque for £3BO, he forged his employers' name, and got it cashed. Lieutenant Percy L 0. Roper, Royal Engineers, attached to the School of Military Engineering, at Chatham, hair been found shot dead At the foot of the stairs leading to his quarters at-Brempton Barracks.- There was a chambei revolver lying some distance from him. The affair is involved in mystery, and has created much excite- ment,, . , There is bad news also for the moneylenders. If Mr. -Chamberlain can possibly see his way to it, he Will Bring in bill to limit the amount of interest recoverable in a court Of law, andlo check in other respects the extortionate prac- tices of Men who live upon the miseries of- their fellow 1 creaturet. The bill would , meet with the assent of all parties in the house. Attention is arawn by the Registrar-General to the fact that the fatal cases of smallpox in London which had been 42, 52, and 54 in the 3 preceding weeks, were again 52 Last weekiand_bac'eeded the corrected average in the corres- ponding week of the past ten years by 3 ; 35 were recorded in the Metropolitan Asylum Hospitals at Fulham, „Hornet-. ton,_Stockwell And Deptford, one in the Highgate smallpox' hospital, and 16 in private dwelling-houses. • A benevolent: ladf-arid- gentleman recently intimated a gift of £130,000 to found a college in Dundee. At a meet- ing of the Dundee High School subscribers, on Monday, ea- -Provost R,obertSon announced that a beneverent citizen' in- tended setting apart-1,30,000 oflris,-fortnne to render the High School intermediate for educational instruction be- tween the public schools, and-the-proposed college, besides establishing a separate bursary fund. .Arrangements were made for taking advantage of the generous offer. , A MATRIMONISL MUDDLE.—A curious occurrence has taken place at Pontypridd.' A man named Moses Evans has just abruptly parted with his "better half" to another per- son—also married—whom he suspected of having too great a partiality for her. He carried her off the street into the Tredegar Arms, and handed her 'to his amorous- rival, remarking-to hint before the company, `."She is' your wife,- not mine; keep her." And keep her the unmentionable has had to.-'

but it does not pay. • oppenheimer reilisedthet his innora, even including his commissions on the sale of paper patterns, I would not enable him to support a wife as wives wish to be supported nów-aklays. What was hi to do? 'He coed not , increase lila income. He must- reduce the expectations of- „ his wife. For that purpose he would use the mighty engine , referred to. The next day hewrote in the 'Fashion Notes:— , 1 "It is no longer bon ton for young gentlemen of fashion to , present engagement rings to their fiancees." Then he went , to the house of Miss Anastasia Pettengill and offered him- self. She accepted him. She looked as if she would have liked a diamond ring; but she said nothing. Next wcek she read in her betrothed's paper :—" Presents between fiahcees are now considered in very bad gout." She sighed; but she said nothing. The next week the fashion weekly said :—" When engaged persons enter an icp cream saloon, it is now-the-fashion for the lady to pay for her own-refresh• aunts." A week after this item appeared :—" Brides this year will dress very simply. Calico is the fashionable ma-- 1 terial." And when the ensuing issue of the paper was laia 1 before her, Anastasia Pettengill read with a breaking heaft this double-barrelled shot : ' Flats are no longer the mode for young married couples. It is considered vulgarly osten- tatious to have more than one room. For light employment' for married ladies, art embroidery is now quite out of date, although in the way of towelling work fine effects may be obtained on a smooth wood ground—a floor, for instance. Fancy sewing, especially in connection with buttons, is much affected." This was too much. When Mithridates Oppenheimer went to seek his bride, he learned that shehad gone into a convent and taken the double-extra black veil, remarking that nothing war left her now to live for. Oppen- heimer has now retired from the fashion weekly, and has now a gloomy but lucrative pp!ition on The Shroud, the organ of the undertaking profession.—Puck. CARLYLE AND IRELLND.—A correspondent sends me the following:—" The late Mr. Carlyle was net to be induced to due out save at one or two houses, and_then on very rare occasions. lam speaking of a time about six Or seven years ago. The few that were invited had a rare treat i for the occasion came but once or twice in the year, notably on a Christmas Day. On this high solemnity a servant was:de- spatched to purchase and select with care a yard-long 'churchwarden,' with a screw of the seer's favourite tobacco, our host finding a pleasure and sacrifice in thus consenting to what was' really odious to him. The Newtown (Montgomerysbirs) Guardians have de- termined to enter into.icontest with the Local Government Board as to the guardians' claim to dine at the workhouse at the ratepayers expense. The auditor repudiated the claim immediately; but the guardians resorted to the device of increasing the officers' rations, and dining off the sur- plus. The auditor discovered. this subterfuge, and gave another warning. This was mot-heeded, and he has n' surcharged the guardians. •. • Sir Henry Havelock Allan, MX., writing to a friend at •Sunderland, says :•—" In A conversation I had on Tuesday 'with Mr. John Bright, I was' stnick with the earnestness, AlmOSt solemnity, with which he expressed his confidence that the forthcoming Land Bill for Ireland would be a standing monument to the labours of the party in the cause of justice and humanity to Ireland, and his convictiOn that it would be such as to satisfy every just expectation of those who desire the peace and prosperity of that unhappy 'country." ' At Manchester, on Saturday, Frank T. M. Kavanagh, des- crilsed as a member or the bar and of several learned socie- ties, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude for con- spiracy, in company with Edward Frith, a solicitor's cleric,'l and a woman named Alice Park, to defraud tradesmen. Firth and Parks wereoach sentenced to 12 months'iMprisonment., Detective-Sergeant Caminada proved a previous con- -viction against Kavanagh, and informed the court that be could bring not less than fifty cases of fraud against the- . prisopers. , At the Glamorganshire Assizes, John Lynch, shipowner, was•sentenced to three months' imprisonment and fined £5OO for sending the ship Herbert, of which he was owner, to sea in such an unseaworthy State as to endanger the lives of those on board. The ship while at Cardiff, in October last, Was detained ' by the Board of Trade, as she. was leaking 3in. per hour. Defendant ordered the captain to proceed, and,the vessel left, but was brought back by a `-steamer sent after her. Her _timbers were rotten, some of them being only *in. thick, and the seams were open.. -- A Bill was publisffild on Saturday. the object of which is to reduce and equalise in all parts of Englan land Wales the fees now demanded by clergymen on the occasion of a burial; and to restrict such fees to the payment for a religions ,service actually performed. The effect of this Bill will be 'that ecclesiastical fees for a religious burial service wiil be kept distinct from the civil expenses incurred in connection with burial. The interests of existing incumbents are guarded by the Act not coming into force in any parish till after the death or removal of each existing ineumbent. The Bill does not interfere with private. rights, nor with. the existing powers ofißurial Boards as regards their ell charges. , FRIENDLY AND INDIISTRIAL SOCIETIES AliD TRADE UNIONS.—The report just issued gives the returns under the Act of 1874 received .by the central office in 1879 for 1878, and of loan societies returns for 1819. It appears that the, friendly societies or branches, not including branches of orders which print their own forms of returns, was in 1878 15,379, of which 12,300 sent in returns. Their members numbered 4,692,175, and their funds amounted to £12,143,609. Industrial and provident societies numbered 1,030, of which 963 sent returns. These societies had 479,002 members, with funds amounting to £5,908,469. Trades unions, nimffiering 177, sent in 124 returns. The unions had 202,984 members, and funds amounting to £309,223. There were 957 building societies, of which 830 sent returns. These..showed a membership -numbering 269,400, with a capital of £28,228,153. The loan societies, numbering 380 i had mem- bers numbering 88,520, and a capital of £122,1430. The grand total of the number of societies is 11,953, of their membership---5,f177,081, and of their-capital f.46f16,614.---H the figures here kiven are compared with thOse of -thelilit summary, printed in the Chief Ttegistrar's report for 1876, it will be found that the present summary shows an increase of 1,621 returns I,s4s,7o7_meinbers, and no less than £18,058,726 funds. Bunn; Feb. 16-,The Lower House of the Diet, to-day, rejected a Marin of Herr Windthorst, the Leader; of the Centre In favour of riScinding the regulations b)'which ..theStale is empowered to withhold -the stipends of recal. citraut Catholic clergymen. Only members of the Centre party, the Poles, and a few Conservatives voted for the motion, while only Ultramontanes spoke during the debate.
The engineers on the Tyne have 'received a general advance of wages. The skilled workmen in the employ of Sir W. Armstrong receive an advance of ls. 9d, and a selected few 2s. _ _

Between 700 and SOO workmen, employed by Messrs. Bolclrow, Vaughan, and Co., Middlesborough, have given notice to leave work in a fortnight should an advance of 5 per cent. not be conceded. • Another large gathering of South Yorks-hire colliers was held -near—Barnsley,--on Wednesday, when-it 'NM unani- mously determined not to recommence work until the full amount agitated for had been generally conceded. At an adjourned conference of Math and South Stafford- shire, Worcestershire' and Shropshire ironworkers, on 'Monday, an inqurince scheme proposed in connection with the arbitration board was adopted by a vote of 20 to 8. Reports received at the South Yorkshire Miners' Associa- tion offices show that there are fifteen pits now working at I advances varying from 5 to 10 per cent. The men at the'l Landhill and Old Oak i Collieries, two of the most impor- tant firma in South Yorkshire, have agreed to . send in 'notices to quit work. The notices pending will add nearly 3,000 more to 8,000 men already idle. meeting of the North Wales oollieries,sliding scale committee, , held. at Wrexham; has, agreed that, having re- gard to the advance in prices which took place in the latter part of January, the accountants be instructed to examine the employers books for the present month of February; and that, in the meantime, in anticipation of the result, an advance in wages of 71 per cent: be giVen as from sth instant. '

At a Conference of miners held at Stoke-oriTrent, oti Monday, attended by npwardis .of 'seventy representatives from different principal collieries in North Staffordshire, the offer of the employers throughout the district to increase the wages 10 per cent. was accepted. The men a fortnight ago: • gave' notice' for an advance of 15 •per cent., and the exrd:, kloyers; who at first altogether refused te accede lo the de- mand, have since offered 10 per, cent, as a Compromise. The wages dispute •in the cotton trade in Ashton-under- -Lyne- has now •been -definitely MUM; A—conferenCe of :employers and weavers was held on Monday night, at which the latter fiuggested that, an tausediate advance of 21 per cent should be. given, and that further advances or reduc- tions should be . regulated by the rise and fall of weavers" wages in North-East 'Lancashire. This arrangement met with the approval of the employers, and the advance will be paid next week. . • .. • . Bind. Association as to paying deputies connected with thstbliners' Association the same rate of wags" members.of theDeputies' Association. The arbitration took place a week ago at Westminster Palace Hotel London Messrs. Am so and Lindsay Wood repre- senting the owners, and Messrs. Crawford and 'Lloyd Jones' the workmen. ' At Stinderland, on Saturday, an anti-coercion meeting, attended by 3,000 persons, was held. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, describing the provisions of the COIIITiOI Bill, said the liberty of every man would be at the mercy not of respon- sible statesmen, but of a hostile magistracy, and perjured ififormtrs and- spies' like Talbot' The limitation of the operation of the Bill to a period 'subsequent ' to 'October Ist, --ttaS io coniprdthise, for that per)od marked the commence-. ment of the Land League agitation. The diminution of evictions was not dueio the Disrurbance Bill which did no,t pass, but to the actiod—brthe Land.. League. Resolutions were passed condemnidg the action of the Government, and especially protesting against the retrospective action of the Bill.

A Dublin journal hat a curious-account-of-a sheriff's sale for rent in county Waterford. Experience having shown that in the present state of Ireland " auetionef Of this nature are complete failures. owing to the absence ot bidders, the Property Defence Association undertook to provide these essentials to a sale, and .nettiallii carried out its offer, its agent "securing ata•very law price-indeed% the entire lot." The defaulting tenant, according to our contemporary, had expected on the failure of the sale to drive. his cattle hack to his farrr4 but the animate were instead-sent-away hy rail, "to the wonder and astonishment and the utter dieiney of the farmers, the Committee of the Land League, and the tenant who had been duped." It is- stated that this defeat of the League is having a salutary effect on the tenants who I are in arrear.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.
div.p: The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock, Cateridnan.—The. Marquis of Hairrniceroie stated in reply to a question that themilitary occupation of candahar and the protection of the line of communication with India would involve an expenditure of two millions sterling a ryear. OPENING PRIVATE LarrEns.—Dr. COMMONS, on behalf of Mr. I'. D. Sullivan, asked the Postmaster-General whether any Officials of the Government were at present empowered to open and read, for purposes of State, private letters en- trued to the care of his department either in Great Britain or Ireland.. Sir W. HARCOURT : The duty of. answering the ;question belongs to the Secretary of State, and not the Postmaster- General, who has' no responsibility in the matter. The power of the Secretary of State to open and detain letters is one which is reserved and sanctioned by Parliament In the statute 1 Victoria, chap. 36, sec. 25, and has been deliberately continued ever since. The employment of that power is an act of the gravest responsibility, not to be exercised except upon urgent necessity' for the safety of the State and Her Majesty's subjects. (Hear, hear.) The existence linown to the Government of treasonable plots carried out by secret societies like the Fenian conspiracy, which pursues felonious ends by the most atrocious means, would justify and require the use °Mitt power in the present as in times past—(hear, hear); but the very nature of the dangers which might de- mand its employment is such as, requires the minister en- trusted by Parliament With the right and the duty of putting it in force to ask the support of this House—(hear, hear)—' in declining. to' make any statement which-might baffle and . defeat the object , for which •it was conferred. (Cheers.) -This power should either betaken away kern the Secretary of State, or, if 'the grave responsibility of possess- ing it is imposed upon him, he should be protected in times like the present in his discretion as to its exercise. (Loud cheers.) —Mr. CALLLN:.,I beg to ask the Chief Secretery to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland—(cries of "Order "and "No,' no,")-.-whether that power has- been or has not been exer- cited towards any metnber or members of this House during the 'present oession. (Cries of "No, no.")—Mr. FolisTen': If I Were to reply to that question it would be in exactly' the same terms as were used by my right how friend -the Home. Secretary. ' (Hear, hear.) , THE .111tramt.—Sir J. HAY inquired whether it was in- tended to embody any portion of the militia in order to render available a sufficient number of full-grown soldiers for ser- vice in the Transvaal and Ashantee wars.—Mr. Cafirmas teplied that no emergency had arisen requiring any such course to be adopted. THE BERLIN Taxam—Answering Mr. Baxter, Sir pus. Din ot stated that the reforms promised by the Porte had either not been carried out or had been carried out in such a iyay• as to depriee them of all the benefits that were =pectic]. - THU' TRANSVAAL "WAR.--lian OHILDEiS read ;r- -tile am from Sir George Colley, dated Sunday. It gives no infor- mation as to Sir George's own position, but contained a satisfactory report from the Administrator of Pretoria and another from Major Standerton, who declared that his force could hold out for two months' if necessary. With regard to the reinforcements, Mr. Childers explained, in reply to Col.. Stanley, that the Government had determinel to send all that Sir Geo. Colley had asked for—namely, 1,500 drafts to the infantry, one regiment of cavalry, and some artillery drafts—and,in addition to these another cavalry regiment, with their horses, and a transfer company of the Army Ser- vice Corps, with their mules.—ln answer to Sir W. Lawson, Mr. Gnaw DUFF made a further statement as to the steps which lied--- been taketr by- the 'Government ht response to President Brand's suggestion. THE PEACE PRESERVATION (IRELAND) BILL.—The coin- mittee on this Bill being resumed, an amendment wee Pro- posed by Mr. RICHARD PenvEn to limit the , action' df the Government to Ireland instead of extending the operation of the Act to England. It was stated that in England there was no such 'Offence as "treasonable practices," and Mr. THOMPSON said that if the meaning of the clause PM' that the Government might take a snspeeted Man away from England, where he would have a fair trial, to Ireland,- where he would be liable to imprisonment without trial,-he efiould vote against it. Upon a division this was rejected by 234 votes to 45. Other amendments were proposed for the pur- pose of securing a- definition, of the offences to, which the bill applies; but they were defeated on divisions by large, majorities. Mr. el,Coesr challenged the Government to say whether a speaker who advised people not to pay theft rent, or not to pay more than Griffith's valuation, would come under the bill; and on this point no very clear understand- ing was arrived at, although it was debated a long time. Mr. FORSTER, when pressed, said it would be difficult to state whether a man who gave certaiu advice which he sup- posed would be followed by the use of ferce and intimida- tion-would come within the meaning of that clause. l:inring • the night the Chairman,' under his new' powers; put a motion to report progress without permitting debate, on the ground that it was brought forward for purposes of Obstruction. . i The House adjourned at 1-25 a.m. . - - HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tuesns.v. The Lord Chancellor toek his seat at 6.0. Arearesr -Amitts.—The Earl of Lyurtaie, recturineto a statement Made by the Duke of Argyll, ,denied chit in throwing a bridge of boats across the Indus, in 1870, he had been moved by considerations of a coming war with Afghanistan.—The Duke of ARGYLL complained that whilst he had received Lord Lytton's intention to raise the sub- , ject, no date had been fixed, and the matter came upon him as a surprise.—After some remarks from Lord BEACONS- FIELD and EMI Gaelevium, the subject dropped. _ THE TRANSVAAL Boxas.—Lord CADOGAN asked 'whether ,the Government were engaged in "suing for peace to the Boers."—Lord Kiln:mum commented strongly on,this way of putting the matter • and : Whilst admitting that negotia- tions Were going on, denied that there was anything like a suppliant attitude on the part of the British general.— Lord BEACONSFIELD defended the phrase used by Lord Cadogan. . Tau Noxious Vale:ions Bitt Was advanced a stage( and at half-past seven their fordshipsadjOurned. - .i• , HOUSE OF-COMMONS,Tuesretv. , Quespoks,—There was only pixteen questions on the paper, and an unusually smelt proportion (only one-third) were put by Trish members with reference to the present condition of Ireland One of these, however, contained seven sub-inquiries, and on Mr. Redmond, who had placed the agglomeration on the paper, proposing without notice to ask an eighth,—Mr. Fonymn somewhat plaintively pro- tested, suggesting that for the present at least the honourable member should be satisfied with the amount of information • ppliede-Another guestionrby Mri•O'Surtavair, led to the. disclosure of the existence of a secret society in Limerick,'' called the Black Diamonds, the dueiness of which was to break windows; smash-shutters, 'and follow the police about whistlingrohnoxious tunes. One of the conspirators had been brought before- the magistrates,. but the cape had been dismissed, which Mr. FORSTER observed was the best thing that could have been clone in the circumstances i Mr. .M'Coaar, whose supplementary appearance was greetedavith , , aprolonged roar, was understood to ask whether this offence I or whistling-oms included in, the retort's presented to Par- •‘- liament. :•,Ml.Foneren gravely answered that 'it was not regarded as an agrarian crime. Tax PEACE PRESERVATION Bttr,o—The House went MO committee and resumed discussion on the amendment moved on Tuesday night by Mr. Callan.--Mr. CLAN desired to have eliminated from the Bill words Which made the warrant Conclusive evidence of all matters therein contained. In the course of a long discussion the Sataarrou-GENEnar. stated that either on report or the third reading words would be added limiting the nature of the conclusive evi- dence to the purposes of the Act.—The amendment was negatived without a division.--In the cense of the discus- sion Mr: CAtLAN went a long way in the direction Of clef} ing the authority of the Chair, but Mr. Flayfair contented him- self with warning the hon._ member.—Mr. Luaus next pro- pos Cel to add a, sub-section providing that every person detained under the 'Act should be permitted to occupy a suitable room with boarded floor, and warmed in winter to a temperature of not less than 613 degrees Fahrenheit.—Mr. DILLort, Mr.O'Surztverr, and other Irish members bore tes- timony to the ill-condition of the Irish prisons, and strongly urged the acceptance of the amendment.--Mr. Foram undertook to state at a later period the mode in which it was intended to treat prisoners under the Act. This overture was, however, rejected by the Irish members; Mr. O'Coswort in the coarse of a heated discussion, being thrice called to order and warned by the Chairman.—Mr, Buieteu subsequently came under the ban= of the-Chairman. The next outbreak led to the actual suspension of a member.—Mr. M'Coax, on rising, deprecated the cries of impatience with which his re-appearance was greeted, by observing g. merely rise to express my inability "—when Mr. WARTON broke in upon the sentence with strident" Hear, hear!" THE PARK QUESTION •-• • • - A special meeting_ of the Se Helene Town Council was . . , held on Wednesday Morning to receive the r special committee appointed to examine itito and consider the sider the reservations and conditions of Mr. S. Taylor'seoffer of a park. There were present His Worship the Mayor ; Alder- men Johnsor, Cook, and Gamble; CouneillorsT. C. Gamble Allen, Twyford, T. Cook, Foster, Mcliechuie, Walker Hanson, Bishop, Belsher, Wilcock, Baxter, Brook, W. W: -Pilkington, and R. Pilkington. The following are the reservations and conditions first offered by Mr. Taylor in' offering to the Corporation of St. Helces a site for public park—lst. Subject to the rights of the London' and North-Western Railway Company the whole of the water to be reserved to Mr. Taylor and his heirs, the Corporation preserving the same from pollution; and, after the expiration of the company's lease, rosintaining the em- bankments and overflow of the Great Dam. 2. Unrestricted right of way at all times for Mr. Taylor and his heirs and the occupier for the time being of Eccleston Hall, and others, by his or their authority. 3. The Corporation to erect and maintain round the. park a substantial wall to Mr. Taylor's satisfaction, and at the point marked A on the plan, to erect and maintain handsome iron gates, and at the point marked B substantial wooden dools. .4. The Corporation to erect to Mr. Taylor's satisfaction, near the point A, a suitable lodge in lieu of the lodge adjoining Sandy-lane, given up by him. 5. No buildings of any kind whatever to be erected within the park without the consent of Mr. Taylor or, hi repre- sentatives. 6. The Corporation within two years to provide an outfall sewer at the point marked C on the plan, each outran to be available for the drainage of Mr. Taylor's estate adjoining Sandy-lane. The following was the report of the committee thereon : Your committee have met from time to time since their appointment, and have given careful consideration to the matters referred to them. Your committee find that of the 37 acres stated to be included in the site offered, the "Great Dam" and "Little Dam," at present held by the L dr N. W. Railway Co, under lease granted the 31st December, 1851, for 50 years, contain, respectively, 14 acres 3 roods and 20 perches and 5 acres and 33 perches, statute measure. Your committee further find that in the said lease Mr. S. Taylor reserved out of the demise unto himself, his heirs, or assigns, all fish and wild fowl, and the sole and free liberty to himself, his heirs, and assigns, and his and their servants, agents, and gamekeepers, and all other persons by or with his or their permission, order or consent, to take all such Lfish and wild fowl as should or might, during the term granted by the said lease, be found in or upon the premises demised, in any manner which he or they might think proper, but so that the quantity of water in the reservoirs was not thereby dimieisbed. The mines and minerals under the said dams were also reserved to Mr. Taylor, with the usual powers and privileges to get and work same, but so as not to draw off or diminish the water. Mr. Taylor also reserved unto himself, his heirs, and assigns, and his and their agents, servants, and workmen, and all other persons by or with his or their permission, full, free, and uninterrupted power and liberty at all times to enter the premises demised to examine the state and condition thereof, or for any other purpose whatsoever. Power is also reserved to Mr. 'Taylor to plant trees or plants in or upon the banks of the dams, -with-certairt-powers and liberties with reference to such trees and plants, and the grass, herbage or produce which may grow or be produced upon the site Of the dams. The lessees' covenant to amend, maintain, and keep the dams and the banks thereof in good surd sufficient repair and condition from time to time, and at all times during the said 50 years. They also covenant to draw off the water from Eccleston Mere before drawing off the water from any of the other reservoirs (Corn Mill Dam, Great Dam, and Little Dam) demised by the Said lease, except on occasions when it may be necessary to draw off the water from the other reservoirs for the purpose of repairing same. They also covenant not to adulterate or pollute the water, nor to draw off without the consent in writing of Mr. Taylor, his heirs or assigns, the water from the dams lower than the low- water level as the same is indicated by a stone in each of the' dams, Your committee have been unable to ascertain the low- water level referred to in the lease, but it would appear that the Railway Company might draw almost all the water from the dam. Your committee being of opinion that the rights of the London and Zlorth-Western Railway Company in the Great Dam and Little Dam and the banks thereof might interfere with the use by the public of this portion of the site offered by Mr. Taylor, have communicated with the Railway Company to ascertain whether they would be will- ing to grant all necessary powers and facilities to the Cor- poration to use during the ter* of the company's lease the Great Dam and its embankments, and to fill up and utilise for park purposes the site of the Little Dane (which, at the present time, is merely a swamp). Members of your cora- mittee and the town clerk have had interviews with the local engineer of the Railway Company on the subject, and, from the engineer's statements at the last interview, it would appear that the Railway Company would be willing to allow the use of the Great Dam and ita embankments on certain conditions, allow the Little Dam to be filled up, and under- take not to lower the water in the Great Dam beyond five feet from the sill of the overflow, provided the Corporation would enter into an arrangement to enable the company to obtain a supply of water from the watercourse of the Cor- poration reservoirs at Eccieston when the Corporation reser- voirs were full. Upon this your committee consulted the Water Committee of the Council, and the latter committee, after considering the matter, passed a resolution that they dared not recommend the Council to interfere with the water supply to the Corporation's reservoirs at Eccleston. Hav- ing regard to this resolution, your committee cannot recom- mend the acceptance of the arrangement proposed by the company. Your committee have been unable, through the necessity of giving Mr. Taylor an answer, to carry the negotiations further with the Railway Company; but the impression of your committee is that the Railway Company would not object to the use by the Corporation of the banks of the Great Dam, other than the artificial banks (which it would probably be necessary for the Corporation to rail off), neither is it thought they would raise, any objection to boat- ing on the dam under certain restrictions. It is-also thought that the Railway Company miglat be prevailed ',aeon- to give up. the site of the Little Dam, and permit_ the Corporation to appropriate and use the same for park purposeL. _ Your committee have had an interview with Mr. Taylor'. solicitor (Mr. Henry Taylor) on the subject Of the offer, and discussed With him the reservations and conditions attached thereto. Condition No. I.—With reference to the reserva- tion and condition Na. 1, your committee considered and urged that some provision should be made for keeping the Great Dam always filled with water from Mr. Taylor's 'aqueducts; that Mr. Taylor should only reserve the over- flow-water; and that the condition requiring the Corporation to preserve the water from pollution should be modified. In reply, Mr. H. Taylor stated that although Mr. Taylor would reserve to himself 04 right fbidraw off the whole of the watet in the Large-Dam after the Railway Company's in- terest therein had expired, it was not his intention to diminish the water in the dam, and thst he would be pre- pared to give the Corporation the best conditions he could .with respect thereto, having regard to the water supply to the Corn Mill Dane and the Eccleston Mere. He also Stated that Mr. Taylor would agree to a modification of the condi- ,tion to the extent that the Corporation should not be respon- Mible for pollotion of thewater by sewage from the Eccleston Hall side of the dam. No: 2.—Your committee considered and urged with- reference to condition' No. 2 that the right of way to be reserved -should be for passenger carriages and foot pas- sengers only, and that carts or waggons should not be allowed; and further, that-the right should be limited to the owners and occupiers of and visitors to Eccleston Hall and their servants. In reply, Mr. H. Taylor etated Mr. Taylor must reserve a right of way for carts, &re., because it was the only way be had from the ball to Thatto Heath, dc. He, however, thought the reservation might be modified with respect to the persons to have the rights.—Nos. 3 and 4. Your committee thought the character of the evalls, lodge, and gates ehoteld be defined, eoascertain the probable cosh- Mr. H. Taylor stated Mr. Taylor would require a substantial fence to divide Ms estate from the Park and to prevent tres- pass: end on the northerly side of the Park (ball end) he would require a substantial wall. The lodge and gates should be equal to those given up at the Prescet-road entrance.-.- No.' g.—Your committee considered that thie condition should be modified so as to except buildinge for Park pur- poses. To this H. Taylor assented.—No. 6.—Your committee objected to this condition altogether, pointing out, that the portion of the estate proposed to be drained was not within the borough, that the Corporation had no outfall sewer in the neighbourhood, and the difficulties which beset the Corporation in the matter of sewerage generally. Mr. ...11...TaYler Stated husply,thatatigresentML. Taylor's land on the westerly side of the site offered 'cirainennto the-pro- posed park, and that Mr. Taylor must have the sewer for use in lieu of such drainage. He, however, said that the time limited. for the makieg of the sewef might be extended' to say fives,r-slx- years, but that in the Meantime Mr. Taylor would reserve a right to drain into the park.—Your com- mittee consider this a very serious condition, as besidei in- volving the construction of a large and expensive sewer in the district at no distant date, the cost of such sewer will be greatly increased by it having to take such drainage, and, moreover, the additional sewage will increase the present difficulties. You's committee instructed Mr. Shaw, land- scape gardener, of Bowdon, to inspect the site and report upon its snisabuityuipaLthe cost of establishing and maintaining same as a Park, and he has made the following Gentlemen,—ln accordance with the instructions of the Town'Clerli, I have inspected the site of this proposed park, and now beg to submit to you itiy report thereon. (1.) I I may say in the first place, that the site possessing, salt does,' the principal requisites of park scenery, is admirably adapted for the purpose suggested. It has natural advantages of surface, facilities for effectual drainage, and a supply of water so abundant that it may be made an important feature tithe laying-out of the grounds. (2.) The place is at present in a rough, wild, and neglected condition: and a con- siderable amount of labour will be required to bring it into order, neatness, and,bemilv, but these are all attainable with- mat any _extraordinary difficulty or 'expense. (3.) The present approach'from the high-road is a good o'ne. Another entrance from Laurel-told seems to use desirable, and also one at East-road. These proposed approaches would not only be convenient for the public, but would enter at points which may be made exceedingly interesting, and by judicious planting and well-arranged walks would break up and

, Aivargifra pa,l of_ the_prOpeTtx state a somewha .... . present drive I t bold and nnpleasing appearance. (4.) The ,44ild to agreat extent retain, but improving the curves througbo graceful lines. , me ut its entire length so as to give it more ' to hit-NM • ,long line of rhododendrons Olieuld be broken 'up in c . thel, rcmontories and recesses,terid these, couabiped wit), grawy ,sopes and expanses, would give. artificial form the drive now pro;ents. (5.) 4 considerable pertion Of the walks already -forme': yiew instead of the, miff and pictueesque varietyao on the ground oould be Utilized, but the curves ehould be improved; and the walks w 'ould require to be so arranged as to eia'm to glide imper- ceptibly- into each other and into the new reads to be intro- Latticed, eo that in every part they may look natural, easy, JAW of graceful outline. (6.), The general surface of the land' could hardly be niece favouratity ionneil for gidng these pleasing pictures of wood, grass. and water so much deaired in grounds of this deseriptioo. It has all the features necessary for laying out to advantage. The grounds are beautifully undulated, and with well laid vat walks could be made a.really charming place. The sunk ground en the left of the drive freer, the main, entrance, shoold be opened out and formed into a grassy ing fringe of shrubbery, th western boundary, which could ' - h with clumps of scarlet rhodeodobteild7rerinelsenpeasillaz!reg.eayiailia°PiPaerr:oatklehathgerde-1 it ' *men trees most suitable and in harrnowywiti Laßen tfihoowrenrstrifr-xishsrwubhs,oitnhreerrspeuprrsiegdhwt or weeping ith scarlet' pink, and white (7.) Green sward being,ene of the principal charms of a situcaltion. park, I would recommend that the land. lying W the main entrance should be cleared and the stuhrelatneegmhir:ehnot! be re delled dered comparatively level 'and sown with grass. extend to the little Dam; which itself might and converted into a" small lake with grassy Inar • s, diversified with clumps and belts of dropping and other aquatic trees and shrubs. Play-grounds might be formed on this land if it should at atty time be deemed advisable. (8.) The land should be cleared of a large portion of the brushwood, the old tree-roots removed, and the undulations of the ground modified where desirable. Glades should be formed here and there for shelter and shade, andclunaps and belts planted for effect; and care should be taken that there are suitable open places commanding views of such parts of the park or its external surroundings as may show prospects gratifying to the eye. There should also be secluded nooks for arbours, seats, vases, statuary, fountains, dm., and all the usual conveniences commonly provided for the accommoda- tion of visitors. (9.) The plentiful supply of water, as I have before raentioned, and the extent ef the great dam may, by judicious management, be made a fine feature in adding to the beauty of these grounds. By careful arrange- ment in the planting of the margins and their immediate vicinity, this dam may be converted into a grand orna- mental lake without encroaching or in any way infringing on the rights reserved either by Mr. Taylor or iha Railway Company, (10.) There will be no difficulty in regard to the drainage, there being sufficient fall from all parts of the grounds to the lakes, the outlets from which are already provided for. (11.) The atmosphere in this case has more , to be considered than either soil or situation, but by a Pro- per selection of trees, shrubs, and evergreens, I see no diffi- culty in planting to good effect. (12.) It is usual to have spaces set apart for play-grounds for girls and 'joys in grounds of this description, but as this is not at present thought necessary, there would be no difficulty hereafter in arranging for them as before mentioned. (13.1 It is not possible to give you an adequate idea of the works herein contemplated without a plan of the same, nor withont it, is it possible to give you more than an approximate estimate of the cost, which in my opinion would be about £5,500, and the cost of maintenance would be about £250 a year.— I am, gentlemen, your obedient servant, Joins' Snow. The Borough Surveyor has furnished your Committee with the following estimate :—Gentlemen,—As desired, I submit you my estimate of the cost of erecting atone wall Pit. high along the boundary of Mr. Taylor's' estate, the erection of a lodge, entrance gates, wood gates to quarry, and a sewer from your boundary to a point marked upon the plan, and iron fencing where it is desirable to keep public off embankments :—Wall along Mr. Taylor's frontage, 970 , yards, £,455; ledge. £75; gates and posts, £100; gate to quarry, £5O; iron railing fence to embankments, £240; about 500 yards fencing, not Mr. Taylor's frontage, £400; !ewer from boundary to E on plan, £250; add for centin• , gencies, £250; total, £3.49s—say £3,soo.—ha4Es HART, ; C.E. • It would appear, therefore, that exclusive of any sewers it may be necessary to make within the borough to comply with condition No. 6, the proposed park would cost from 0,000 to £lO,OOO for its establishment, and £350 per an- I num for Its maintenance, and that the total annual charge noon the rates in respect of the park, would be about £l,lOO, made up as follows :—lnterest on £lO,OOO at 4 per cent, £400; sinking fund, say £350; cost of maintenance, £350; total, £1,190. Representing an annual rate equal to from iv. to Xlid, in the X. Your Cnmmittee in submitting this report, beg to leave the matter of acceptance or other- wise of the offer for the decision of the Council. The TOWN CLERIC said he had been in further communi- cation on the matter of the reservations, and that morning be had received the following letter:— Dear sir,-1 have perused the report of the Special Commit- , tee, of the 3rd, which you handed to me on Saturday last, and In reference to the reservations attached to Mr. Taylor's offer have to observe—lst, In reserving the water Mr. Taylor does not intend to reserve the right to draw off the whole or any of the water in the great dam after the expiration of the Rail- way Company's lease, but as stated at the interview he reserves the right to use all surplus water passing over, and if necessary, at the level of the waste weir. Mr. Taylor has always contem- plated the great dam being kept full as an ornamental sheet of water; and although, as stated to the committee, he will not guarantee that the dam shall be so kept at all times, he hones that arrangements may be made to keep it full so long as It re- mains water tight, and there is no such flow than that caused , by the evaporation. sec dreservations, thour cannot prepared to to. momentm y oso this iftdetlnmeeeexxarjyt the persons to whom the right should be limited. I may further state that it is not intended to reserve the right so far as carts are concerned to other than the owners and occupiers of Eecleston Hall. The other conditions referred to in the re- port do not appear to call for remark. You will please not forget that Mr. Taylor looks to the Corporation to make the necessary arrangements to meet his wishes respecting the Pad- dock Dam and the new reservoir.—l am, yours faithfully, HENRY TAYLOR. The Town CLERK: Mr. Taylor expected that thel Cor- poration would give up all alleged right of fishing or skating on the Paddock Dam and the New Reservoir. ' A MEMBER: Does the water of the dams belong to the Corporation? i - Tim MAYOR: Yes sir; be said it had been a nuisance, and he requested it to be settled now and for ever, so' that there might be no more questions arising out of it. Mi. T. Coox : But it is not made a condition. , • The MAYOR: No but be decidedly objected to'coshing or skating. , Towst CLERK: He has always for the last 25 years, objected to the corporation fishing there, and he now ex- pects if they accept the offer that there will be no further question and that no role be permitted tellsb on the paddock dam and reservoir, He said he had no objection to skating - - on the reservoir. Mr. HEMMER : Which is the new dam ? TOWN CLERK : It it called leg of mutton dam. The MAYOR said that before they proceeded to further I consider the matter he would ask if it was desirable tat the reporters be present. He should like to take the opinion of the Council on the question. Mr. PRIBILER: rthink they ought to stop. , Mr. R. l'lmruscrrox said the position was this. The Council would go into committee on the question of the offer, and a great many things no doubt would be said and a great deal of information given and necessarily. so, as they were accepting the park on great responsibility. They ought to look upon the matter as a private business tran- saction, Mr. Taylor being one of the parties and the cor- poration the other. He thought it was desirable that the reporters should retire, and he would move a resolution to that affect. i Alderman GAMBLE seconded the motion, and said Mr. Taylor had pude a very generous offer certainly, but there were conditions attached to it which would have to be dis- cussed fully, and it would be very disagreeable to Mr. Tay:, lor to hear an adverse discussion op 'what be thinks a very favourable offer, although everything snigbt be said hi good faith, and necessary to the consideration of the subject. Alderman Jonarsoar's personal opinion was that the re- -porters should be present;- as the subject was oue of irast im- portance to the ratepayers, whe would Imve to bearche 4- penses. Not only so, bit fraln titan tetimi:reports got into the papers, and very often defective reports, and a true ver- sion of what is the real case should not be Withheld from , the public. • As to the probability of a discussion being dis- agreeable to Mr. Taylor, he (the speaker) theinght heought .to know the grounds upon which the Council accepted the 1 gift if they did e 0... . Mr. McliEcßait spoke in favour of the reporters staying, but if there was anything which should not be made public they could be Sasilnasked net to report that. Mr. l'inxixavolt expressed his willingness, seeing the feeling of the Council, or a portion of it, to withdraw his motion, if the seconder agreed. Alderman GAMBLE said he was agreeable, and the Coun- cil having resolved itself into committee, Mr. R. PILKINGTON said it was very desirable to have one, ..---, Orrlliree piilis- When the town could afford it. The cost of the park was a little under stated. It wasalmost impos- sible to give a proper estimate before anything was done in the way of construction. f-. 5,500 was put downte as the e probable cost of the laying out, and the yearly main £250 a year. But there were several other things. The very cost of the sewer might to be included £1 , t_2oo. and ry likely there would be some outlay in widening he embank- ment of the Big Dam, because the people would want to promenade round round that bank, and it would make a very good one. On the north side the land was very restricted, and it would perhaps be found necessary to make that side larger. There were two approaches to the park besides the one in Liverpool-road, to be made, and he put down for those £1,400. The maintenance of the park Would cost more than they thought. The estimate he had put down was £5O for a park keeper, and £259 for the gardener and his assistants. Plants, manure, and seeds he put down at £100; and £3O he put down, thoup,li small, for maintain- ing the banks; £BO tor painting and general expenses. The' total sum he thought to be expended on the park was £14,000, and the maintenance £7OO. That would give the cost to the borough of something like 2d in the A. It would be_vely much nearer the figure than that in_tharepott. It was a pity they had not the 37 acres entirely in the power! of the Corporation, and that Mr. Taylor's friends should go ' in at any time and interfere with the rights of the Corpora- tion. As to the North-Western Railway Company, they would get rid of themyin 21 years, and until that time had , expired the Corporation would of course have to "grin and bide." There was a feeling that the company would deal with the Corporation in a liberal spirit; brit after every-

thing had been signed, sealed, and delivered,7lo thought it would be very difficult to get them to do anything. He did not think they mir any. company would be willing to make any alteration in than Pi:Avers. Ai to the right of Mr. Tay- lor to the water. .It was hie whole of the, water at first ; but he had made an amendment, whereby- he took all that , went over the weir. That. made it a great deal better, but he (Mr. Tilkington) very much preferred that they should at the end ed the 21 years buy it out and out, so that the Corporation-Should not be under his power at all. The Cor- poration had now to keep it free from pollution, and thus there waste probability that Mr-Taylor would be interfering at times with the Corporation,•. • It would be far better and more satisfactory to the Corporation that they should free theinselves from any liability. They Must remember, in taking those liabilities, they were to be borne also by those *eialietag after them, furl br, 21 years' time he could not tell whit the lialfilities would be. There W 55 no doubt that the value of the land and the water would rise considerably; and in 21 years' time the borough would probably double itself, around St. Ann's a large esimmunity would be growing, and if they did not, Wee care enregard t they o that water question ey would put t...awselves ma peaition to be a source of revenue to Mr. Taylor. --Hethou tit far , more -desirable to clear those liabilities oft by ng Mr.' Taylor what was the price of thoserestrictina a ,useera.. , dons, so that they might have 37 aces as the property of n4h the public of S. Helena entirely. Mr-Taylor had ne doubt been actuated by generous motives, and it was exceedingly desirable they should have a park, but if the doper was the meet public-spirfted man, the most genevous and good man, he would not advise the Corporation to commit themselves to anything which suggested the possibility of a law suit at 'swine future period. Mr. Pilkington was proceeding to speak ' of the coal underneath the' park,. when The TOWN CLERK- said: He does not propeee to reserve the coal. He reserves the minetout of the lease to-the railway company, but he does not propose- to reserve the coal from the Corporation. . Alderman GAIVIBLE said it did not occur to him it was rpossible to ask Mr. Taylor to deliver the Corporation fron the liabilitiea spoken of by Mr. Pilkington. It was a very good idea of Mr, Pilkington's.. He had his own feeling about the 'natter. They would want to make an agreement —5.-legal instrument—by which this-property would be made over to them, and he thought they never would be able to agree to the words of that agreementS He did not think Mr. Taylor would. As far as their interview with the solicitor went, it appeared that the words about the property and water laid down so distinctly had an exactly opposite meaning. It was stated all the water was reserved, and it was in that representation that the committee succeeded in getting it modified.. Mr. BAXTER did not think the people of Parr could afford to give 4d. in the pound towards a park at Eccleston. If it were desirable to carry the negotiations farther, he was quite of opinion that they should try and get the park entirely freehold. Mr. H. PILKINGTON said there was no doubt a park woald always cost them a great deal of money. Although it was . out of the town it Was close to the best suburbs Of the borough. It would have great advantages even if it did cost 2d. in the pound. By making St. Helens a residential place they made it a solid community, an 1 they would induce the rising respectable part of the people to remain in the town. , They ought to face the question of a perk, and make it a residential place fit for the working and other classes. Alderman Jontrsow said Councillor Pilkington bad given very good reasons why they siniuld have a perk, and the present proposed park was one very well adapted for the purposes of enjoyment, when the bulk of the population could go out for a walk on a Sunday afternoon. It was a very convenient place, and in a short time, when the tram- ways were completed, it would be very easy indeed to get to the park. He did not agree with the figures of Mr. Pilkington altogether. As to the cost of putting the ground in order, £5,5Q0, he should have expected when they receive this park that they would engage a person as head man and 500 under him, to clear away and put the park in order, as suggested by the landscape gardener. But this should be going on gradually. What were those men to be em- ployed in? It would be principally on Sunday the park would be used, and if they took the park, and began gradu- ally.to lay it out, the cost would not be so much. As to the47oo for maintenance, he thought that was too Touch. He did not see what painting there would have to be to cost 1380 a year, and, as to widening the embankment, that could be done easily. £l5O for materials and repairs was much too, high. .As to the objection against Mr. Taylor having the binerflow,' he did not think they would be any the worse for that, as the water did not belong to the Corporation. There might be a little more objection to Mr. Taylor's carts going through, but that would not be a very great injury. One condition vow that the land on the westerly side was to be drained. Ile thought that was a very objectionable clause at first, but, after it had been explained by the Town Clerk, they had nothing to complain about. The reason was this—St. Helens was increasing; and they-would' have to provide a sewer in that part before long. ' - Councillor Emma thought it Would be quite as Well to see Mr. Taylor again. He was very much in favour .of a park; but, at the same time, they ought not to allow their !zeal for the public health to override their discretion. They ought to do all they reasonably and possibly could for the health of the people, and snake the borough a place in which a healthy life could be`lived. . The TOWN CLERK observed that Mr. Taylor would require a definite reply by the 23rd instarn; as ht had-extended* the time twice already. . Alderman Gennza said if Mr. 'Taylor would give them the upper part of the land It would be much moreesatis-, factory. Alderman Jonsson and Mr. McKraterne said it wpuld be a mistake if they did so, as the land they now effered 'them Iwas the best part. Mr. R. PILKINGTON moved, "That it appearing from Mr. Hy. Taylor's letter to the Town Clerk, of the 15th instant, that Mr. Samuel Taylor was disposed to make some modifi- cations and concessions as to the reservations and conditions attached to his offer this meeting, be adjourned until Satur- day, and a special committee be instructed to communicate with Mr. Taylor as to such modifications, and:see if 'he will grant the whole of his rights, and further whether he me:mid give to the corporation the land of the proposed site - other than the Great Dam without any, or, it any, what conditions." ....., , , Mr. BAXTER seconded h h the motion, which was c . div.head: ten4lag
div.p: time of peace, of such a force in garrison at Candahar would be £90,000; but that "taken with reference to the military and political conbiderations for main- taining each a force beyond the frontier" it would be "double that amount." Now, is there any English. men, not a soldier or a Government official with a selfish eye to profitable appointment, who will assert his opinion that the retention of an advanced mili- tary post at Candahar is worth to this country and to our Indian Empire £2,000,000 a year in perpetuity, or even £1,000,000 ? We don't know; there may be a few such persons, for most singular crazes on questions oi our foreign policy do possess certain minds. But in Lancashire, where as we have pointed out, the issue is very distinctly between a pacific military attitude on our Indian frontier and a retrenching movement in Indian finance on the one hand, and the continuance of the tax upon the productions of our principal industry on the other, we cannot believe that there will be more than one opinion as to the necessity for the former procedure on the part of the Anglo- Indian Government. The impulse, however, to such a movement must be given by the Home Govern- ment; for the IndiartExecutive will never enter upon a course of systematic thrift in finance, with the object of abolishing protective custoni duties, of their own good will. On the contrary, they display a spirit both of wrath and spite on seeing that this Government, following out in this regard at any rate the purpose of the last, has determined to foster free trade between England/ and India by sweeping away at the first opportunity the tariff impositions which hamper trade. Bearing therefore in mind the amount of active or passive resistance the Government encounters in India, both in its measures for cementing peace and for reduoing etpencliture, in order to get rid of taxes injurious to the trade of this country, we ask our readers to reader all the political support they can to the Government whilst engaged in carrying out these objects; and not to be induced by any specious representations whatever of the war party to join their voices in any demonstration in favolir of the relation of Candahar which may perhaps be attempted. The two millions a year saved by quit- ting that part of Afghanistrn may eventually be worth to the commerce of Lancashire with India, by providing for its liberation from fiscal fetters, several times two millions of money.

HisTata, ancient and contemporary, makes us ac- quainted with the fact that in all ages of the world women have not infrequently played an important part in political and social struggles. Nor have their contributions always been only in the nature of moral support to the sides on which they have ranged them- selves. During the Freneh revolution "the ladies" were a power not to be despised; and, in these modern days, some of the ablest and most determined of the leaders in the Russian insurrectionary movement which we know under the name of Nihilist are from the ranks of those who have been poetically described as the "softer sex." Then again, when we look across to Erin's Isle, we see that the ladies are about to take part in the agitation that is going on there. Unfortunately, we have a bitter social struggle going on in Lancashire between the miners and their em- ployers. Hitherto the males have been the moving spirits in the agitation, but they now appear to be backed up by the "ladies." In many of the struggles which have taken place between workmen and their employers in former times we have heard workmen's wives condemn the strize, and have been satisfied that if the issue had been left in their hands they would very quickly have settled the dis- pute by telling their ,husbands to resume work. But in this struggle it seems that the sympathy of the women is entirely with the workmen. On Saturday last about 2,000 women assembled in the Market Place, Pendlebury,'where they were addressed by a number of their own sex, who were very en- ergetic in insisting that their fathers, husbands, brothers, and sons should be encouraged and supported in the present crisis. One miner's wife declared she was ready to perish with hunger before surrendering, as they had lived long enough on " herrings and dry bread." This is not what any one would regard as sumptuous fare, and we have no doubt that miners' families have had to put up with very "hard limes " recently. But they are not singular in this respect : for, in- deed, there are many other working people in this busy world who have had to be content with wages quite as low as that of the miners, and in some cases even less remunerative. lieverthless it should not be forgotten that the miner Whilst toiling in the bowels of the earth for the " biaohdiamond '" is in hourly danger of losing his life by any of those sad mishaps which so frequently occur in collieries, and it is therefore only just that this enormous risk should be taken into account when .deoiding the remuneration he ought to receive for his labour. It cannot therefore be denied that the miners are acting strictly within their rights when they claim that this risk should be considered, and that they are entitled to higher wages, and that the women of Lancashire also have a perfect right to support the men in this agitation. Bat we would remind these.good ladies that there is ouch a thing as moderation. Whilst no one will object to "Nan" Morris advising the colliers" to take in washing rather than go down the pit for the paltry sum they got," we can scarcely imagine that the language used by another woman to the effect that "if anyone would give her a gun and cap she would shoot the masters, and id -they were all of the same mind as her they would go to Worsley and not leave a brick on the hall," is at all calculated to advacce their cause. Violent and abusive language will only tend to alienate the sympathy of the public from those who use it, and we -sincerely hope that we shall hear no more of it.

Ix will be seen from the report of the annual meet- ing of the Warrington Conservative Association, which appears in another column, that the Tories of Warrington are bestirring themselves and doing their utmost to complete and perfect their organisation. They have appointed a "most admirable man" as their political agent, and have actually succeeded in raising a subscription list of nearly £650 per annum.? With these means at their command they boldly announce their intention to change the representa- tion of the borough at the first opportunity. The treasurer of the association, however, admitted that he was in the unfortunate position of having "to -commence the year with a large balance against him," for out of the £650 promised he will have to pay last year's registration expenses, and the expenses of the municipal election. We should like to know whether after discharging these liabilities he will have a .balanepeeion people mighthandora bssa.ylance against the association. Some whole of the liabilities should it in not made known nhat the that no balance sleet was produced, but of course that could not be the reason. The bulk of the money already promised came irou! vice-presidents and others who gave two or three guineas each, and although they had not yet reached to the subscribers of smaller must be bwe g e aroeodt,olfdorthcaatpttam he plesrapeoictasahmaosnygesry t tohoeisie. siderately came forward and stated that he should be happy to pay the annual subscriptions of is., 2s. ' or ss. for any of the men in his ward who could not afford to do it themselves. Ras the gallant Captain read the new Corrupt Practices Bill? If he has not s t tvotes edt() done so we would recommend him to give it a careful perusal. The crushing defeat of the Tories last April was attributed by several of the p given by Staffordshire men and the Irish inhabitants of the borough. Is there any disgrace eake r s t attached thech these two sections of the community? What is it thathas made Warrington what it is to-day, in spite of Tory Opposition and musty Conservative ideas? What has caused it to emerge from a" nice agricul- tural town of about 20,000 people" into the present thriving, manufacturing centre? Is it not the iron trade? And are not the despised Staffordshire and Irish workers referred to by the Tories, the very men who have by their honest labour contributed so

div.head: EXAAIINEE, SATURDAY FEBRUARY l9, 1881.
div.p: largely to this result—a , result which has enriched many of these Tory grumblers as well as Liberals? Is it not a great reflection on the old Warringtonians that they are still—according to Captains Litton and Reynolds—as Conservative as ever they were? It would appear to us, from the language used at the Conservative meeting, that the Tories regard War- rington as their own peculiar political freehold, and that no matter how many thousand men may come here to reside, and thus contribute to the increased wealth and prosperity of the town, the list of voters must exclude all but Warrington men. Such narrow minded ideas belong to the dark ages of the past, but will not be accepted by the educated and enlightened classes of the present day. We are therelore pleased to Team that this remarkable display of bounce and activity on the part of the Tories has been for some time anticipated by the Liberal party, who are fully alive to the circumstances, and we would impress upon each individual Liberal the necessity of watch- ing to see that the Tories do not rob the Stafford- shire, the Irish, or any other workingmen of the franchise. Let each man to do his part by seeing that his own and hAs neighbour's names are on the list of voters, and any information that may be required will be gladly given and received by the active and energetic secretary of the Liberal Associa- tion, Mr. Henry Roberts.
HOLY TRINITY (RUNCORN) YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.—An assay was read on Monday night last by Mr. R. Yates, on 'Elijah," and a very interesting debate ensued.
BEUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUN- CORN-Mr. Charles •Garnett, gave an interesting Bible lesson on " Jesus of Nazakh," to the members of this class.

ZION MIITITAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, VvrIDN'ES.—An entertainment of a miscellaneous character was given in the Zion Schoolroom, Widnes, on Tuesday night. The Rev. John Billington presided. HALTON MU TEAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. At the general meeting, on Monday evening, Mr. W. Edge read a paper on " Trials and Triumphs of early Christian Martyrs." The paper was very interesting. The following gentlemen took part in the subsequent discussion :—Messrs. T. Miller, R. Hughes, A. E. Davies, and S. Barrow. The Her. J. Bateman presided.

Sr. VALENTINE'S DAY AT RUNCORN.—Somedays be- fore the advent of St. Valentine's, notices were freely posted in the district by instructions of the Runcorn Postmaster (Mr. Lea) requesting that the devotees of the saint would post their missives early on the 12th inst. This appeal was very fairly responded to, and a large number were posted on the Sunday—probably on the principle of the better the day the better the deed. However, we must not be over critical in a case where one of the tenderest emotions of the human soul is concerned; and to say very much upon this point would probably bring down upon us criticisms from a considerable number of the fair readers of the Examiner. It appears from our inquiries that the number of valentines posted compares favourably with that of last year.
