A CARE OF BIGAMY: ONE OF TILE MARRIAGES AT RUNCORN Pantsn Cnoncw—At Liverpool City Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. Raffles, Mary Barnett, 23 years of age, was charged by John Searle with bigamy. Detective-inspector Cozens, in opening the case, said : "This is a case of bigamy, Sir.. Three witaesses. The first was solemnized at Runcorn in 1874; and the other in Liverpool. We are all ready. Let them be sworn." (Laughter.) John ' Pugh, a dock labourer, was called and said he was present in the parish church of Runcorn, on the 20th April, 1874, when the prisoner was married to John Searle, who was now in court. The next witness was the second husband, Richard Barnett, a seaman living at 93, Stanhope-street, who proved having been married to the prisoner at Holy Trinity Church, Parliament-street, Liverpool, on the 7th of August last. He had been courting her eight months previously, and she represented herself to be a single woman. Police- constable Smith (456) said he arrested " Mrs. Barnett "at 93, Stanhope-street on the 12th inst., and charged her with bigamy. She said, in reply: "To tell you the truth, this man (pointing to her first husband) made me do it. These marks I got from his abuse." She now pleaded—" Well, Sir, I could not live with my first husband. He abused me so. He is so short-tempered no one could live with him." The prisoner was committed to the assims for trial, Mr. Raffles intimating that he would take bail—two sureties of .£2O each

AN ADVENTURE WITH A DRUNKEN MAN AT RUNCORN. —A correspondent sends us the following :—An amusing, but at the same time a disgusting, scene took place in Run- corn on Saturday last, giving a striking example of the way in which Bacchus treats many of his votaries. Anyone passing St. Paul's Chapel, High-street, at about 3-30 cm Saturday afternoon, might have seen two partially drunken men endeavouring to carry a third man, whose worship at the shrine of Bacchus had evidently been more devoted than that of his companions., One of the men had hoisted him upon his back, while the other walked behind, carrying the feet and steering! After proceeding down I-Ugh-street, this ludicrous cavalcade turned along Mersey-street, when the rough pavement tripped up the foremost man. The three men then fell to the ground, in a bewildering mass of ragsearms, legs, and heads. Two of the men next scrambled to their feet, and each took an arm of their helpless comrade round his neck, while another carried a leg under each arm. Thus the comical procession moved on. They had I not gone many yards, however, when the fellow's braces, which had for some time shown symptoms of weakness, under the severe strain now put upon them by the foremost man carrying his share of the burden by the trousers, finally gave way. How these poor fellows would feel on recover- ing their proper senses, after so violently kissing mother earth, Jam not able to say, but I sincerely wish that they may have been reminded of the litres of Burns : Oh ! wad some power the giftie glens, To see airsel's as itbers see us. It wad fra many an evil free us. And toolish notion."

A aronvvax Dim:rm.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Field, the case of Regina v. Inhabitants of Abram, came on. The counsel for the plain- tiffs (wko were, amongst others, the trustees of the Bicker- shaw estate, at Abram, near Wigan) were Mr. Addison, Q.C., Mr. Heywood, and Mr. M'Connell (instructed by Jeans and Hepherd, of Warrington); and for the defendants (the Local Board of the district) Mr. Gully, Q.C., Mr. Leresche, and Mr. Crompton (instructed bv Messrs. Peace, Ackerley, and 'Co.). The dispute arose on the question as to whether the landowners of the district or the Local Board (acting for the inhabitants) were liable for the repairs of a certain road known as Bickershaw-lane, sheeted in the township of Abram. The lane was two miles long, and it connected the two important highways—one called the Warrington-road, leading from Wigan to Warrington; and another called the Wigan-road, leading from West Leigh to Wigan. Plaintiffs argued that this road had always been a highway—there were public-houses and farmhouses upon it—and it was con- tended, therefore, that the Local Board were liable to keep ,it in repair. Evidence was called to prove that Bickershaw- -1 lone had been used as a highway 50 years ago.—On behalf lot the Local Board, Mr. Gully stated that they were per- fectly willing to adopt the road and take it over as a high- way, providing the rich landowners .of the estate, to whose collieries it led, and by whom, therefore, it had been chiefly used, were willing to put it in a -state of repair first.--Mr. Thomas Bankes, a mining engineer and surveyor at Leigh, and one of the trustees of the Bickershaw estate, admitted that the trustees were the real plaintiffs in this matter.— Ins Lordship interposed, and appealed very strongly to Mr. Addison to come to a settlement. He said the parties would probably spend more money in costs than would put the road in repair, and he thought the money would be better spent on the road than upon the learned.counsel. (Laugh- ter.)—Mr. Gully, on behalf of the Local Board, said they were willing to pay £5OO towards putting the road in repair' providing the landowners would pay the remainder, which would probably be another 4.500.—His Lordship considered this a very fair offer.—The case was then withdrawn until the next assizes, in order that, in the meantime, an arrange- ment might be come to. - -

WESLEYAN METHODISM a.x Wmzrns.—On Monday evening, a tea meeting was held in the Oaklanthstreet Wes- leyan Methodist Chapel, Widnes, for the purpose of in- augurating a movement to reduce the debt upon the chapel and erect a new place of worship. There was a fair atten- dance at the tea, and a public meeting was afterwards hel4, at which Mr. Robert Shaw, of Higher Runcorn, presided. On the platform were the Revs. C. Bingant (superintendent), J. Tesseyrnan, and Messrs. B. Brown, W. Hartland, and T. Whitby.—The Chairman first called upon the Rev. C. Bingant, who, after briefly referring to the object of the gathering, said that seven years ago arrangements were entered into with the Chapel Committee in Manchester for wiping off the debt upon that building. The amount of the debt was now £920, and year after year had passed away without them doing much to pay off the ncumbra nce. After some futther remarks of a general character, the speaker concluded by saying that if the necessary sum for paying off the liability were raised within 12 months the Chapel Committee had agreed to contribute £3O towards the object.—Mr. Hartland said that at the meeting of trustees it had been suggested that they should get a number of papers printed, and endeavour to obtain volunteers amongst their friends to go round and collect donations. Subscription forms would also ibe handed to them at that 'meeting, and the amounts pro- mised might be paid at any time daring the ensuing twelve months. He felt certain that if they determined to throw the requisite energy into the movement for extinguishing tke debt it would prove snccessful.—The Chairman was of opinion that they would find the raising of the sum re- quired a Very simple matter if they would all work with a wilt. He wished to guard them against one mistake, viz., that qf borrowing money. He did not know whether any of them had ever been in the habit of borrowing money and promising to pay it back at the end of three months, but if it were 60 he felt mire they had always found that at the end of the required period they had felt it as difficult a mat- ter to pay off the debt as it would have been to have wiped off the original sum on account of which it was contracted. He did opt think that any one of them would be any poorer by that time 1882, if they decided to give to God's cause that night. Subscription papers were next handed round, and sums were promised in amounts varying from is. to £7. The total amount promised was £6o.—The Chairman then observed that he thought the best course would be to adjourn the meeting until March, in order that they might be able to obtain a larger attendanee of friends and take even more definite steps.—This suggestion was unanimously agreed to, and the proceedings terminated. A description of him appears in the Police Gazette. Locer, BELLS IN PARLIAMENT.—Against the South- port and Cheshire Lines Extension Railway Bill petitions have been entered by the Birkdale Local Board, the South- port District Highway Board, the Corporation of Southport and Mr. Thomas Currie Mather. WIDNES PARLIAMENTARY DEBITING SOCIETY.—At this meeting, on Wednesday evening, the adjourned debate on the Government Land Bill was resumed. The Foreign Secretary, the member for the city of Gloucester, and the Premier took part in the discussion, after which the bill was read a second time. The House then went into committee on the bill. The first clause was passed without dissent, and the second clause after considerable discussion; after which the debate was adjourned. I

RUNCORN, WESTON, AND HALTON WATERIVORES' CO.— The report of the directors of this company, for the half- year ending 31st December last, has just been issued. The document, which is signed by Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., as chairman of the Board of Directors, states that the revenue account shows a balance of £S4G 19s. 6d., including the amount brought forward from the previous six months, out of which a dividend of £5 per cent, per annum, free of Income Tax, is recommended to be paid. This will absorb £523 55., leaving a balance of £323 14s. 9d. to be carried fsrivard. Cram= Cr ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY : RUNCORN BRANCII.—On the removal of the Rev. Mr. Anderson, curate, from Runcorn, the branch of the Church of England Tem- perance Society in the town last its secretary, and for sonic time past it has been in a dormant state. Our temperance readers will be pleased to hear that Mr. Rogerson has con- sented to take the position of secretary. The first meeting of the Band of Hops was held at the National Schools on Wednesday evening, when Mr. Shaw, seamen's missionary, occupied the chair. DEATH OF AN OLD WOMAN AT WIDNES.—MT. C. E. Driffield, the county coroner, held an inquest at the Market Gate Inn, Widnes, on Saturday, on the body of an old woman, named Mary McGrath, aged 72, who died on the previous Wednesday. The evidence showed that deceased was in receipt of parochial relief, and she was taken ill about eight o'clock on Wednesday morning, and died im- mediately afterwards. Evidence was given by Mary Smith, the woman with whom McGrath lived, and deceased's son, Bartholomew Burns. The jury returned a verdict of "Died from natural causes."

DEATH OF MRS. PETERS, OF WIDNES.—it is with sincere regret we have to announce the death of Mrs. Peters, wife of the Rev. Thomas Peters, minister of the Milton Congre- gational Church, Widnes. The deceased was well known and highly respected as an earnest Christian during her re- sidence in this town. After an illness of a few days dura- tion she succumbed on Monday night last, leaving a large family to lament the heavy loss they have sustained. The interment took place on Thursday morning at Farnworth, the funeral service being conducted by the Rev. Geo. liol- loway, the vicar, and an address delivered by the Rev. J. Yonge, of Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington. THE WIDNES WELSHrWESLEYANS.—For some years the Welsh Wesleyan Methodists have worshipped in a small building on the Marsh, bat this became too small, and the one in Cromwell-street was built. For some time past the need of a more centrally situated chapel has been much felt, and the members of the congregation having carefully considered the proposal, found that the site and building would cost about £1,200. It was agreed to make an effort to raise £BOO, after doing which the friends considered a start might be made. Amongst the subscribers are Messrs. Gossage and Sons £25, Mr. T. Robinson £2O, Mr. J. W. Carlile £2O, Mr. Edward Roberts £25, and Mr. Richard W. Roberts £25. Several firms in Widnes and Runcorn have promised donations.

WIDNES PADISII CM:MOIL MUSICAL ENTENTADMENTS. —The tenth of this series of entertainments was given in the National Schoolroom on Tuesday. Three glees were rendered by the choir, "The belfry tower," "The iron- founders," and the "Huntsman's chorus." The pianoforte and violin performances of Mr. J. S. Gabriel and Mr. R. Gabriel, of St. Helens, were features in the entertainment, as were the two songs by the first-named gentleman. A reading by Mr. J. B. unison, a gnartet (" Bells of eve ") by Messrs. Fairley and Broad and Messrs. Wilkinson and Ire- land, and two songs by Mr. F. W. Wilkinson, were the other items in the programme. The Rev. T. Wright Williams presided. OLD MEN'S SUPPED AT HALTON'. The old men resident in the parish of Halton were entertained at supper at the Norton Arms Hotel, on Tuesday. About forty par took of a capital spread, the Rev. J. Lockwood mesiding. Among the other gentlemen present were Messrs. R. Holland (agent to Sir Richard Brooke), Thomas Wright, John Smith, sen., Stokes, Thomas Acton, William Nixon, C. W. Brown. Supper over, the Chairman suitably addressed the old men, and afterwards proposed the health of the Queen and other members of the R0y...l Family. This having been duly honoured, the Vice-chairman (Mr. Holland) gave the health of the Bishop and Clergy, and ministers of all denominations. He coupled with the toast the name of the Rev. J. Lockwood, who responded. The health of Sir Richard and Lady Brooke was afterwards heartily drunk, as was that Of Mr. Thomas Wright, the surviving promoter of the annual treat ,to the old men. During the evening Mr. Haddock sang "Jim the carter." Mr. Holland also gave "The whistling thief." An enjoyable evening was spent.

HEALTH OF WistumaroN.—The Medical Officer of Health (Mr. Gornall) reports for the week ending, 12th of February, that 48 births and 19 deaths, including 3 at the workhouse, 2at the fever hospital, and 1 at the infirmary, have been registered. On the estimated population, includ- ing Latchford, of 40,000, the birth rate was equal to 5911 in the 1,000, and the death rate 241, against 43.6 in the cor- responding week of 1880 and 35•1 in 1879. The deaths of persons under 5 years of age were 2, and under 1 3, 40 9, and 130 and upwards 5. The total of 19 deaths includes 1 from malignant smallpox, 1 from enteric fever, 4 from tubercular disease, 3 from lung diseases, and 10 from all other causes. The proportionate mortality from preventible diseases was 31 per cent. There has been no case of infectious disease reported during the week. Piraimrrtral. FE:num.—The following petition lies for signature at the Warrington Liberal Club:—To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain and Ireland in Parliament assembled. The humble petition of the under- signed showsth, that there are several perpetual pensions of large amount now charged upon the consolidated fund or annually voted by your honourable House: that some of the said several pensions have been paid for the past 200 years: that in some cases the origin of such said several pensions has been entirely unconnected with any benefit or service to the nation: that in every such instance of perpetual pen- sion the Amount already paid has far exceeded the value of any service alleged to have been rendered to the nation by the original grantee: that in some cases the conduct of the original grantee of such pension has been the reverse of meritorious, and the original grants of such pensions are utterly indefensible on any ground of public policy: Your petitioners therefore pray that your honourable House will direct careful enquiry to be made into the circumstances of the original grant of all perpetual pensions now paid, and whether or not such pensions are charged on the Consoli- dated Fund, and also as to the circumstances under which each of such pensions is now paid, and by whom and why each of such pensions has been received from the date of the original grant (when the reciPisnts of any_of such pen- sions axe not the direct heirs of the bodies of the original grantees), and that your honourable, House will, where necessary, repeal any statute and will cease to pass any vote under which such pinsions are respectively payable.

div.head: LOCA.L NOTES,
div.p: Those of our readers who have made a practice of care- fully conning the reports of that lively body of gentlemen known by the name of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, will have observed the frequency with which discussions have arisen as to the difficulty experienced in obtaining pay- meat for services rendered by the Fire Brigade to people living in the out townships. It certainly must have been veryirritating to the Commissioners to find that when they have conferred a favour, which one would, at first glance suppose would be properly valued, those who had re- ceived it would be only too ready to show their thankfulness. Men who have, however, studied more carefully the workings of that strange piece of mechanism known as the human mind, will not be at all astonished to hear that in numberless cases the very people who have found the assistance of the brigade so inestimably valuable in their own particular case have been the last to dream of paying the hard-working fellows for their services. All my readers who have arrived at mature age must have come across instances in their own particular experience showing how delighted many people appear to be if they can succeed in hiding every trace of having received a helping hand from some kindly-disposed friend, who might very easily have left them to shift for themselves on the highway of life, which, if I remember rightly, my friend Lamb says is strewn with flowers for some, whilst others have to tread it with bleeding feet. This, I believe, is commonly known as kicking down the ladder by which you have succeeded in rising. Those who have been made victims of any such supposed clever fellows may take this consolation to heart, that, " Th.mgh the mills of God grind slowly, Yet they grind exceeding small; Though with patience He stands waiting, With exactness grinds He all." It is gratifying to know that the Commissioners have de- termined to stand no more of such nonsense as that to which I have referred, from their so-called friends in the out townships, and that those gentlemen who have for some time been "lingering shivering on the brink," as far as their pecuniary liabilities in the case of fires upon their premises were concerned, will in future receive "the due rewards of their deeds!" Some short time ago I understood that cer- tain rules were to be drawn up as to fixed charges being made for the fire engine going a certain distance, and that no start would be carried out unless an undertaking were signed to pay the expenses, in the case of all fires occurring outside of Runcorn. lam not sufficiently well posted to be able to state whether this scale of charges has yet been drawn up or not.

Whilst upon this subject, I may briefly notice that at the Runcorn police court, on Monday, a Kingsley farmer was summoned for non-payment of £24 55., being a charge made by the brigade for attending at a fire on his premises, on the 4th inst. Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the Com- missioners, and consented to an adjournment on the ground that the insurance company had agreed that a cheque should be drawn for the money at the next meeting of the directors. Though I have noticed this case, I would not have my readers conclude that the farmer in question is one of the recalcitrants to whom I havezeferred, as it is quite possible he has done all required Of hint, 'under the peculiar circum- stances of the case.

The members of the Widnes Property Owners' and Rate- payers' Association mustered in strong force at the annual audit of the accounts of the Local Board, on Wednesday morning last. Several of them addressed Mr. Darlington, the auditor, in the way of compaint, that on application having been made, they had not been permitted to see a con- siderable number of docennents they were desirious of inspec- ting. I hear that matters at first presented a somewhat threatening and formidable character, as one hero after another entered, so to speak, the breach, like another Horatius, to uphold the liberties of the people. The auditor appears to have taken a very prosaic view of the matter, for instead of treating the appearance of the deputation as a subject fraught with the greatest moment to the Widnes commonwealth, he, rattler phlegmatically, told them that it was very certain he could not grant their request to be I allowed to examine the books at that particular time, as he could not have the atedit interrupted. He, nevertheless, treated the representatives of the Association in a very gentlemanly manner, and promised to consider their com- plaints on the following Tuesday. It is stated that Mr. Staveley Hill, M.P., is drafting a bill to provide for the compulsory inspection of house property. Such an announcement ought to strike terror into the breasts 0 the numerous " jerry builders" who put up buildings in Widnes and Runcorn. There are rows of cot- tages, and even of a superior class of property, in both towns, which though fair outwardly, are as deceitful as the Pharisees of old, inwardly. No doubt some people are of opinion that the author of -"The Stones of Venice" has " a bee in his bonnet" on some subjects, but there is one in res- pect to which they can heartily sympathise with the master of English pose, and that is the way in which a great deal of work is scamped. The day appears to have gone when the working men of this country took a pride in turning out an article which should be a recommendation for English goods, whether it was found in the lonely hut of some settler in the far west, or on the snowy peaks of the Himalayas. So it is with the erection of buildings. A man decides to put up a number of cottages; several contractors are asked to send in estimates, and the one gifted with the greatest shrewdness often joined to a wonderful deftness in leaving undone what he has most assuredly led the owner to expect he would do, proves suezessful in getting the work to do. By-and-bye a wonderful name is put up at the end of the row—a name which is often as deceptive as the Eden in which Martin Chuzzlewit found himselt, with se sad a heart; and the eager tenants take possession. Those who I imagine their friends have been exceedingly lueky to secure I one of the houses, pay them a ;visit, and they hear most doleful tales of the various inconveniences which those whom they thought were favoured mortals, have been put, owing to the abominable way in which the builder has done I his work. It may be said that suth dwellings wuuld not be I put up if there was not a call for them. I am, however, sure that they would remain empty if better houses were to be had. What is wanted is that our smart and loagheaded friend the jerry-builder should be .firmly held to certain conditions in the carrying out of his work, and I am sure my readers will share with me in the hope that there is truth in the statement as to Mr. Stavely Hill's intentions.

The latest return as to the foot and mouth disease, show I that 67 animals have been attacked in Cheshire. At the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, a master butcher, who appeared much astonished at being brought up on such a charge, was fined as the owner of a number of sheep which I had been removed from Frodsharn, after an auction sale, and were found in charge of his servant, who was not In possession of the necessary certificate. I hope my Runcorm readers will not forget that Mr. Ras- took Pierpoint's ballad concert takes place on Thursday evening next. In addition to Mr. Pierpoint, who is at present a student at the Royal Academy of Music, Miss Eleanor Falkner, pupil a Mrs. Sims Reeves; Miss Emilie Lloyd, of the Royal Academy of Music; and Mr. H. S. Bywater, of the St. James's Hall and Crystal Palace Concerts, will take part. -

Last week the Runcorn iaatmen in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Company were out ort strike, in re- spect to a question which it seems is not quite of such vital importance as they imagided when they ceased work. Some of the older men, who thought the game they were playing was hardlylworth the candle, advised the general body of the men to try to come to some amicable settlement with Mr. Meadowcroft, the general manager, and the other gentlemen associated with him in controlling the traffic. Mr. Thomas Norman, who is at all times ready to put himself to a little trouble in a good cause, was asked to act as dip- iomatist, or shall I say plenipotentiary, to what I may describe as the Bridgewater Court. He consented and the little difficulty was soon settled owing to the forbearance macifested on both sides. It is a pleasant thing to see that the men are now all at work, and matters have resumed their accustomed appearance on the canal. FL ACCUS.

TIM CASE OF STEALING PIGEONS.—James Walsh, youth aged 16, was charged with stealing two pigeons from I the premises of Mr. Robinson veterinary surgeon, Simm's • Cross, under circumstances lolly reported in last week's Examiner.—James- Hardman and Thomas Bagley, both lads, and Thomas Cecil Robinson, son of the prosecutor, gave evidence, and the prisoner, who pleaded not guilty, ; was fined 20s. and costs, or, in default 'of payment, one month's imprisonment. Scwoon Bosun CASES.—Several persons were convicted, on the evidence of the school attendance officers, Johnson and Woods, of not having sent their children to school, and had each 59. to pay.—Mr. Denby, the clerk, appeared to prosecute on behalf of the School Board. THE APPLETON INNKEEPER AND HIS WIFE.—Mr. Harri- son Turton appeared in custody, on remand, charged with, having committed an aggravated assault on his wife, Catherine. The facts ef the case have already been fully teported.—Mr. Beasley said he now appeared for both corn- plainant and defendant, and he had to state that since the last adjournment he had been instructed by the twq people concerned to endeavour to bring about some arrangement. Accordingly, on the previous Monday, a deed of separation was executed, and the complainant was now willing to withdraw the charge with the permission of the Bench.— Mrs. Tinton was called, and corroborated the statement made by Mr. Beasley.—The Chairman said that he and his brother magistrate were glad to hear that an arrangement had been come to between the parties. It was understood that the prisoner would not go near his wife, and he hope d that some arrangement had been made as to the mainte- nance of the defendant's *child.—Mr. Beasley said the de- feudant would be entitledto see his child four tames a year. —The Chairman &tit; he hoped that if the hints thrown out as to Mr. Turton having given way to drink\ were true, he would uow try to turn over a new leaf.—The prisoner was then discharged, and left the court with his friends. Tim TOPERS' Mar.—Bernard Donnelly was fined 55. and costs, on the evidence of P.C. Peddar, for having been drunk and disorderly in Victoria-road, en the sth instant.— Thomas Norman, greengrocer, was charged with having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart in James- street, on the 10th inst. P.C. Stott gave evidence in the case, and defendant was fined 10s. and costs, or, in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—For being guilty of this offence, on the 10th hest, John Talton, Victoria road, who did not appear, was fined is. and 4s. costs. P.C. Palmer proved the case. THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR AND His Dc-TIES: WARNING TO ROUGHS.—James Quinn, Joseph Hardmann, (who did not appear), and Edward Farrell, were charged with maliciously using defamatory language, calculated to promote a breach of the peace, against Mr. John Dickson, sanitary inspector to the Local Board.—Mr. Beasley ap- peared to prosecutor, and said that part of the duties of the complainant were to see that the contractor for the removal of night soil carried out his work properly. For a long time past youths, and in some cases grown up people, had made it a practice of making offensive remarks to Mr. Dickson shout his occupation, as he went about his work. The matter had at length become so intolerable that it had been con- sidered necessary to issue summonses. Mr. Dickson had no vindictive feeling in the case, but the nuisance had pro- ceeded so far that it was necessary a stop should be put to it. Complainant was then called and gave evidence clearly incul- pating Quinn and Hardman; but the Bench did not consider the evidence against Farrell, who called two witnesses, was sufficiently strong to establish the case.—The Chairman said the summonses against him would therefore, be dismissed. The other two defendants had rendered themselves liable to imprisonment, or to being bound over to keep the peace. It passed his comprehension why the young men should have conducted themselves in such a manner. The ratepayers were considerably taxed for the purpose of appointing an officer to look after nuisances and see that the neighbour- hood was brought into a wholesome add healthy condition.. Mr. Dickson was appointed for the purpose of seeing that the provisions of the Public Health Act were properly enforced: and rather thaa annoy him they ought to sympathise with him.. Those who continuer/ to do so would be severely dealt within future. The defendants, Hardman and Quinn would each have 7s. ed. and costs to pay. Tenrusray.r-Before Mr, F. H. Gossage.

ALLEGED COAL STEALlNG.—Margaret An Dawson, a married woman, was remanded until Wednesday next, on a charge of stealing 581bs. of coat, the property of Messrs. Evans and Co., from a wagon on the Marsh.

• RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MorrOsi.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick (chairman) and Mr. James Reynolds. ALLEGED NON-PAYMENT FOR SERVICES OF THE FIRE BRIOADE.—Mr. Stephen Ravenscroft, farmer, Kingsley, was su.nmoned by the Runcorn Board of Commissioners for non-payment of £24 55., being the charge made by the local Fire Brigade for attending a tire at the former place on the 4th November last.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, law .clerk to the Commissioners, appeared on behalf of that body, and said he did not think it was necessary for him to go into the case, as he had simply to apply for an adjournment until next Monday. A letter had been received from the In- surance company stating that at the next meeting of the directors a cheque would be obtained for the amount. If the money were paid on the following Monday, the sum- mons would be withdrawn.—The Bench granted the appli- cation for an adjournment.

- OFFENCE UNDER THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (AN-Imam) Acr BY A WIDNES Burctmt.—Mr. Richard Baxter, butcher, Mersey-road, Widnes, was summoned for that he was the owner of five sheep which were being moved from Frodsham to Runcorn by one John Webster, in contravention of a certain order under the provisions of the Contagious Dis- eases Act, 1878. John Webster, a man in the employ of Mr. Baxter, was also charged with having offended against a certain order made and published by the Privy Council,' under the Act mentioned, by removing the animals.—Mr. Baxter said he did not consider himself guilty, as he did not know that it was necessary to have an order for the re- moval of the sheep.—Mr. Ashton, magistrates' clerk : Igno- rance of the order is no excuse.—P.C. Bossons said that on the evening of the 10th inst. he was on duty in Bridge- street, and met the defendant Webster driving five sheep. He asked him where he had brought them from, and he said from a farm called Bradley Orchard, near Frodsham. In reply to another question, Webster said he was going to take the sheep to his master, at Widnes, by means of the ferry. There had been a sale at the farm mentioned the same day. The sheep were taken to the public slaughter- house in Runcorn, and killed there, an order for that pur- pose being granted by the police. Superintendent Williamson said he should like to say that Captain Arrowsmith, the Chief Constable of the county, had taken a great deal of trouble to make the various orders of the Privy Council, and the provisions of the Contagious Diseases' Act, thoroughly well known in the district. Notices on the subject had beed served on the owners of cattle, and also posted in conspicuous places all over the county. Ile was at a loss to know how the defen- dants could plead ignorance of the law, under the circum- stances—The Chairman said the ignorance pleaded by Mr. Baxter was no excuse. He could not very well understand how it was the defendant Baxter, being a butcher, did net I know of the regulations. The employer had made himself liable to a very heavy penalty, but the Bench had decided to only inflict the small fine of 20s. and the costs, in the hope that the publication of the case would act as a warning to himself and others concerned. Any butchers who offended in like manner in the future, might depend upon it that the fine inflicted upon them would be much heavier. As to the man Webster, he had no doubt that he had acted under his master's orders in the matter; but still that was no excuse, and he would be fined ss. and costs.

ROBBERY BY A LAD.—Jameslobinson, a boy aged 14, was charged with stealing four ounces of soap, the property of Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst, on the let inst.. Robert Keogh, an oilman, employed at the works, said he was at work there on the evening of the Ist inst., at about six o'clock. an 4 he saw the prisener come off the Bridgewater canal bank, go to the soap pan, and take out a piece, value one penny. He fol- lowed, caught him about the bottom of Vicker's-street, and brought him back to the:manager.—Mr. Samuel Pope, mana- ger at the works, said the firm did not wish to press the case, but he might state that they were very much troubled with boys coming into the works, both during the day and night, and they could not proceed against them as trespassers.—The Chairman said that in the hope the prisoner would be more honest in future, the Bench would only fine him 55., includ- ing costs, or, in default of payment, three days' imprison- ment.

FRODSHAM. Lteruitu Fat&usu.—On Tuesday evening the Rev. H. Valentine, of Runcorn delivered a lecture in the Trinity Wesleyan school-room, 'Chapel-lane, the subject being "Queer Folk." The Rev. F. F. Edmunds presided, and there was a good attendance. A collection was made at the close in aid of the Band of Hope. FRODSHAM METHODIST FREE CHURCH MISSIONS.--On Sunday last two sermons were preached in the Methodist Free Church, in aid of the home and foreign mission., by the Rev. J. Billington, of Runcorn. Sermons were also preached on the same day at Kingsley, by the Rev. R. Trotter, Frodsham. The annual meeting was held at Frodsham on Monday evening, when addresses were deli- vered by Revs. R. Trotter, F. F. Edmunds, and H. Borwick. Mr. J. Booth presided. The annual meeting at Kingsley was held on Tuesday evening, when Mr. A. White presided, and addresses were delivered by Rev. R. Trotter, Messrs. Samuel Walker, J. Booth, and U. Parker. a DARING HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT FRODSHAM BRIDGE.—A daring highway robbery took place on Wednesday morning ewt t o about w n , half-past Frodsham, four was on Wednes- day going to at Frodsham Bridge, the facts being that as a man named day morning, he was stopped on the Sutton side of Frod- sham Bridge by seven men, who came from Bailey's hedge, WestonWlliani chemical Hancock, works, f N a and enquired if he had anything upon him, two of the gang taking hold of him, one wrenching his arm back, which caused him to shout. They thereupon desisted from violence, and searched his pockets, bfit finding nothing a knife was produced to cut the rope with which he had tied his day's provisions on his back. Seeing what they wanted, he offered to untie the rope, when they took the handker- chief containing a saucer and his food, drank his tea, but returned the can. They then left him, and went in the direction of Warrington—Hancock being only too glad to get away, and returned home. The men were strangers, and appeared to bail from Lancashire.

div.head: LATEST TELEGRAMS. ecc:-
div.p: THE OLDHAM OPERATIVE TWINERS' STRIKE. As the Oldham operative twiners, who are out on straits, will not give way, the employers have determined to try females to do the work About nine of the mills women have been taken on with considerable success.

THE CONVICT DAVITT. - The Home Secretary has granted permission to Dr. ha. Cs Kennedy, of Dublin, Mr. Michael Davitt's physician, to visit the latter in Portland Prison, in order to ascertain the exact condition of his health, and what medical treatment, if any, is required by the prisoner. Dr. Kennedy will pro- ceed to Portland on Monday next. THE REPRESENTATION OF EAST CUMBERLAND. At a private meeting of the Conservative party of East Cumberland, in Carlisle, yesterday afternoon, Mr. Jan3et Lowther, late Irish Secretary, was formally adopted to con- test the vacancy in the division in opposition to Mr. George Howard. The Sheriff has fixed the nomination for Wedaes• day next, and the polling for the following Saturday.

div.head: MURDERS
div.p: A coroner's jury yesterday returned a verdict of wilful murder against Thomas Brown, alias Slater, for killing Sarah Ross, with whom he cohabited, at Union-street, Borough, London.—George Moore was charged, before the Gravesend magistrates, yesterday, with the murder of Mary Ann Marsh on Monday last. Prisoner WRS remanded for one week.

div.head: CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL
div.p: A deputation from the National Liberal Federation, headed by several members of Parliament, including, we understand, Mr. McMinnies, M.P. for Warrington, waited upon the Attorney-General at the House of Commons on Thursday to urge upon the Government the advisability of making certain additions to and alterations in the Corrupt Practices Bill now before Parliament. Sir Henry Jamee replied at some length, and promised that the matters re- ferred to should have the attention of the Government.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: ROUSE OF LORDS. Crarrmir. AmA.—The Duke of ARGYLL made an expla- nation as to the bridge of boats and the assembly of troops qn the Indus in 1.878.—Earl Lyyrrox denied ,that he had in 1876 planned an invasion of Afghanistan, or an at- tack upon Russians in Central Asia.—Earl of Nowlin:m(3oX justified the course taken by the Duke of Argyll.—Viscouct CitaNnaoox asserted that the bridge of boats and the col- lection ef troops on the Indus were never intended for the invasion of Afghanistan.—Earl KIMBERLEY:Said that the want of Candahar had led to these accusations.—Ead GRANVILLE contended that the accusations brought forward had been substantiated.—Earl BEACONSFIELD insisted that the policy pf the late Government had been entirely justi- fied, and the accusations brought had been entirely refuted. —The subject dropped. CAsnmy.B.—Lord lArrrow postponed his motion OA Candahar until Monday week.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE WAR IN THE TRANSVAAL.—Sir G. CAMPBELL gave notice that on Monday he will ask if the Government have sent any terms of peace to the Transvaal.—Mr. GLangrobra said it was not until the 20th December that the Govern- ment had information that the Boers meditated rising, and on getting that news troops were despatched on the 23rd. EXCLUSIVE DEALING.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said he had no information that a combination had been entered into with , the city of London by two firms for exclusive dealing. . CANDARAII.—The Marquis of Hererrwcirow, replying bo Sir W. Palliser, said it was not proposed to ask the Gover- nor General of India to form an estimate of the troope required to hold Candahar. If it were proved that the retention of Candahar would materially add to the stability of the Indian empire they would be willing to review the whole question. That, however, was not likely to be proved....

Homins asked the Speaker for an explanation of the new rules an- nounced the previous night.—The SPEAKER deferred his answer until the next sitting of the House. THE PEACE PEESERVATION BILL.--The House went into Committee on the Protection to Persons and Property (Ire- land) Bill, and the Cuatisstax ruled that more than twenty amendments standing on the paper in the names of members of the Home Rule party were inconsistent with the bill, and passed them over accordingly, amid great cheering.—Mr. METGE and Mr. LEAHY then moved amendments which were also ruled by the Cumititsx as irrelevant—On the question that the first clause as amended stand part of the bill, the Committee divided with the following result:— Ayes, 302; Noes, 44.—0 n clause two, Mr. COWEN moved an amendment to provide that the warrant of arrest should also contain the grounds on which the Lord Lieutenant based his suspicions.—Mr. Pousrxrt opposed the amendment.—

MANCHESTER Corrox.—There has been rather more business put through this week than recently owing to the low prioes which sellers have been induced to take rather than run too nearly out of order. The improved tone of the cotton mrrket which became manifest on Wednesday has deterred sellers from going into further orders at the level touched. There have been no really extensive purchases, and buyers seem very slow to persuade that any advance is possible in view of the good sup- ply of cotton and large production going forward of both yarn and goods. The very large import into Liverpool this week raises the stock of cotton into upwards of three-quarters of a million bales. The prices ruling is, however, considered quits reasonable in view 01 the consumption, and generally speakiqg the demsnd for goods is regarded as quite healthy. LONDON PRODUCE. THE WARRINGTON RATEPAYERS' OASSOCLA'rION. - Sir,—lf the object of the above Association bens stated— *To promote an economical expenditure by the spending 0-3*— power of the town, and try to regulate the rates and taxes," ▪ c it ought and will, I think, have the sympathy and assistance nem . of the great body of the ratepayers of the town. If carried on upon these lines and with this object, it will be worthy of Its name; but, judging from the array of names in your re- poet, it appears to be narrowed into a Shopkeepers' Associa- -4- tion for the protection‘of their own interests and the pre- • vention of cheap buying. The great cry of these very e,d; respectable gentlemen is about the marketiand the cheap buying there is in it. Now I never hear of any complaints irom ratepayers who were not shopkeepers. The general ' public who, I think, are ratepayers, find no grievance in being able to go into the Rag Market and buy cheaply what they would otherwise have had to pay dearly for. This so Called Ratepayers' Association must not expect to have the rag: great body of the non-selling ratepayers with them if they ..,1 Darrow their object in this way. They advocate the imposi- tion of prohibitive tolls on the stalls of the "Fag Market." This would mean higher prices for purchasers at these Stalls; the extra price being in effect a tax upon the rate- payers who buy here, in order to keep up the pride of the shopkeepers whe will not themselves take these standings, t and, by underselling, run these interlopers off thi ground. 't Political economy teaches us to buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest; but the Warrington Rate- ., payers' Association wish us virtually to tax ourselves in • seder to do away with the cheap market, so that we may have the inestimable privilege of buying in the dearest. In these days of free trade this antiquated injustice of taxing one part of the community for the protection of another is . a notion not likely to meet with favotir;at least from those who are to be taxed. I have always understood that the • Rag Market was one of the best paying concerns under the 1, Corporation management, even with the stalls at a half- 2. crown toll. Then what kind of commercial morality is it that !, proposes to sell at 15s. what yen can sell at a profit at 2s. 6d.? , If these g,-Dtlemen have a grievance in this matter the remedy is in their own hands. Let them take these stalls themselves, buy cheap and sell cheap, and the thing is done. —I am, etc., JOHN PEERS. Warrington, February; 14th, 1881.

As one of the deputation an- ; pointed to wait upon the masters, I ask permission to say ▪ through your columns what I would have tried to say on the kir ground. • (1.) rwould have given an emphatic denial to the state- ment that the representative miners were refused an inspec- " tion of the pay sheets. There was no refusal. In the "case of Messrs. Bournes and Robinson, the miners were present when Mr. Byrom laid his statement before us; and hi, the other cases I fully believe that the books would have been 41' as open to the miners as they were to the other members of 1r- the deputation if permission had been asked. I very much regret that it was not. It was thought It" the time sufficient - for the the Mayor, Dr. Twyford, and myself to make the ' examination. r, (2.) With reference to weekly pays, if I had been at the -4' meeting I would have asked whether it is not true that this S „thange, which the masters are willing to grant, will be W; .41a equal to an advance of at least 5 per cent. I' know that „ihr s nfiners think that it will; some think that it will be worth —*ten more-. ' ' (5.) I would also have urged the acceptance of the pro- ...„c• .",posed ballot at each colliery. This ,is surely the fairest way; Indeed I venture to think it is the only way of • getting the'opinlon of the men all round. lam acquainted • haa with a number i of miners who never go near the mass meet- • fogs. It s only right that thesenhould have an opportunity • &id ,• :of voting, and that those who think it useless to prolong ' the present struggle should have an opportunity Of !eying •i• so without feat of suffering at the hands of their fellow-work- I need hardly say how deeply I sympathise with the oge, s• 'collier. 'Bis work is toilsome and unpleasant, and he de- to be well paid for it. N 3 one disputes that the wages of colliers are low, and most heartily should I rejoice if '.they were raised. But wages are regulated by the state of the market. When the price of coal is low, wages must be low. Now, I believe it is a fact —it was made very clrnr to the deputation that previous to the strike • coal was more than 20 per cent.' lower than in Jane, ok7) 1877, when the last reduction in wages was made. That is to say, the.price of coal has come down more than sti,j4o per cent., while '*ag** We'onv como-down 10 per cent. .scoL It is aLsd vrell atteSted fact that there are collieries in ibis (.6r :district which are working--or were up to the strike--.not that .only with no profits, but at a gveat loss. Under these 'dr- ' curostaneesi I cannot see how a rise in wages can be • • pected. If the Miners were appealing to the benevolence 1:t, 'Of the masters and asking for charity, their present action - "'Would be -justifiable. But it is, justice, not charity, that atter.l... they are asking for; • and there certainly can be no injustice ma, in the law .witicis makes wages depend- upon the state of *** trade. Every day that the strike • continues will make the. - state of tradeworse, nnd will teed to blight that promise of reilvat which we were beginning to see. To my mind • Magi's a-grim and 'sorrowful suggestiveness in , the word -get,• "strike.", To strike is to deliver, a, blow ; and the histoty AWL e striloes is a history of blows aimed unwittingly, • but net as the less injuriously, at the prosperity of the nation.- •Under * theses blows, if they are repeated often enough., we must ere • long ks a reign go down ; and worst of'rdl, from these 4.."2. div.p: ----- . , NOVEL DEMONSTRATION. . A novel and interesting demonstration in connection with the minere,striketoOk place on Saturday on the market ground, Pendlebury, when 2000 women assembled. Eight colliers' wives ascended a cart and addressed the crowd. A Mm. Clayton presided, and advised them to stand firmly by their husbands during the struggle. Mrs. Broadbent said they should encourage and support their husbands whilst a drop of blood remained in their bodies. Let them perish with hunger ' before surrender, as they had lived long enough on herrings and dry bread. (Applause). The public distributions et soup tickets and provisions have been stopped, and many private in- dividuals'have been compelled to discontinue their relief, finding that they were unable to etuffinue so serious a drain on their pulses. MEETING AT WIGAN. • A meeting of Lancashire miner delegates, representing the whole of the union, was held at Wigan, on Wednesday, , at which it was decided by 40 to 16 that the miners should remain out until their demands ' are conceded. The non- unionists also held a meeting and determined to ask to be allowed to resume work at weekly pay, an advance of wages not being pressed. , . 'INTIMIDATION BY COLLIERS. About 200 'colliers on strike at New Seaham colliery on Wednesday,marched to the houses of some of the men who have continued at work. Several of the 'Men were severely beaten, and the furniture in their homes was smashed. The

div.head: COLLIERS' STRIKE AT ST. HF,LEN S.
div.p: COLLIERS' STRIKE AT ST. HF,LEN S.

The strike at St. 'Helens, judging by the feeling exhibited at the meetings, and the unyielding attitude of the masters, does not give promise of an early termination, but it is felt by many that the miners will return to their work now that the masters have firmly and decisively refused to grant any advance in the wages. At the end of last week the detach- ment of soldiers stationed at the Volunteer Hall was substi- tuted by the 108th Foot. On Wednesday, at twelve o'clock at noon, a meeting was held on the Fair Ground to consider the report of the deputation which had waited upon the masters. The deputation consisted of the Mayer (Alderman Harrison), Dr. Twyford, Rev. R. J. Ward, and three miners. A report signed by the three first named was posted through the town, and read as follows:—" The Colliers' Strike.—We, the undersigned, having been deputed by the miners of this district, at a public meeting of the 12th inst., to wait mpon the colliery proprietors of this neighbour- hood, have to report—(l) That the majority of the masters called upon by the deputation are willing to pay their men weekly if the men desire it, but decline to make any other concession. (2) That the prices of all coal since 1877 has been gradually falling from that time to December, 1880. (3rd). That we find on carefully examining the books at the Wigan, and Whiston company's offices, at Messrs. Bonrne s and Robinson's, Sherdley colliery, at Messrs. D. Bromilew and Company's Garwood collieries,' that the wakes paid to the men employed at their collieries ayerage over ss. per.day, and we regret that we do no see any pros- pect to advance any wages until, a revival in trade should seem to warrant it. James Harrison (Mayor), E. P. Twy- ford, R. J. Ward." The report was reed with great dis- satisfaction by the colliers.. ' Mr. Cnoss addressed the meeting on Wednesday evening, reported to the' men the result of the deputation to the masters. Mr. Evans could net give the advance, and referred them to Mr. Benjamin Glover, and that gentleman said the same. lie (Mr. Cross) said that if they had taken Mr. Evan's prices they would have .found them larger than those of the other collieries, as he wee the regulator nf the coal market in that district. Wigan and Whiston coal company replied that their men earned ss. a day according to the books, but they did not allow, the men's deputation to see the book, and only allowed the Mayor and the other two gentlemen that privi- lege. The price of,coal supplied by that fon onght to give to the shareholders a fair per centage, for Rushy Park coal was ss. 4d. a ton, the highest price ever charged during the last 35 years in ordinary times, and other com- panies bad paid good dividends at that price. But he (Mr. Cross) conaemned wide work all through the country. The nextplace they visited was Messrs. Bournes and Robinsons. 'Their coal was selling as nigh in the market as ever, it had done during the last 25 years. They said they could not' give the men advances, but they would give weekly pays. They (the men), however, said that if they had taken the last month's prices, instead of 1880 prices, they would have found that those prices in the two months' were as high as they Were in 187/, and would have given the men 15 per cent., which would have answered equally as well as a sliding seals, because there was no sliding scale so just as that caused.hy the value of coal in the•market ; and had the masters %en honest they wpuld have advanced the men's wages the same as they advanced their Coals. Messrs. BroWnlow s reply Was similar in effect to the Other.--Ultimately a resolution Wes put to the Meeting and carried, that they remain out. • The feeling among the men in regared to the alleged re- fusal of the masters to allow the' mirers' deputation to see the books and pay sheets is expressed in no measured terms, and they say if the masters can show that the men were getting ss. a day of eight hours they are willing to 'accept 4s. 6d. a day of nine hours, and go to work on Monday morning; and if they will allow Mr. Cross and an accoun- tant to examine their 'pay sheets, and it is shown that the men are earning ss. a day, .they will return to work at once. A reply has been recaiived, however, from the Wigan and Whiston Coal Company, stating that they won't allow any such inspection. It reads as follows, and will be read with interest and some amount of curiosity , From Wigan and Whiston Coal Company (Limited), Presoit, to Mr. T. Glover, George Hotel, George-street, St. Helens.— We will allow any respectable person to see our wages sheet, but not Mr. Cross, or Mr. MoH.lnley, or Jacob Atherton. We are surprised that you shnuld doubt the integrity of the Mayor and other gentlemen.—Yours respectfully, for the ComPii9Y, TI/OMAS FETAINGTON. A meeting'of miners was held on Thursday in Batterhey's room, near Ram Pit, Ilayaock, and a vote by ballot was taken whethei they should work or play, 93 per cent.voting for the motion to remain out on strike. A meeting was held at the Wagon and Horses Inn and a resolution wae carried that they remain out until they got the advance and weekly payments. Several men returned to work at Messrs. Evans' colliery when they found that the Permanent Relief Insurance Clause wee to be in operation, but they refused to accept it and came back.

The new ConseriYative Government' assembled on Friday evening, Dr. McNicoll (the Speaker) presiding. The minis- terial statement was read as follows '

Getitiernen,=thr] Conservative Ministry has accepted offree With a proper sense of the responsibilitied entailed upon it, and-the Ministers now lay before you a 'statement of their, policy in regard to foreign and domestic affairs. 'The policy' of the Government iii regard to the -Eastern Question will be to bring about a settlement of all the out- standing difficulties on the lines of the "Treaty of Berlin; and to avoid a renewal of hostilities, they will use every endeavour to induce Greece to accept any offer of the Sublime Porte which may seem reasonable, and which, above al', is 'in accordance with the wishes of the subject popula- tions interested. In the Transvaal, energetic military measures will be taken to suppress the revolt of the Boers, and to re-establish British authority. •In View of recant events, the Government deem it indispensable to•retain pos- session of the frontier accorded to its by •the Treaty of Gundamack, and also to'continue the occupation of 'Ganda- , bar. At an early date the -Financial Estimatet will be submitted to the }louse, providing liberally, but not extra- vigantly, for the•vations departments of the State: ISug. gestions will at the same time be made for the readjustment of Taxation. The state of Ireland has given.rise to great anxiety. on the part of the Government. ' The .practical 'suspension of the Executive Government there, the increase of agrarian crime, (other than murder) the extended system of terrorism throughout the country, and the inadequacy of the ordinary law to meet the emergency have rendered it teceSsary,for the Gbvernment to ask this House for excep- tional legiSlationiand measnres for the restoration of law and Order, and for the better protection of life and property:. in 'that cottntry will 'at Once be slbmitted to you. • Yon will afteritarda be' asked to consider Measures of a remedial character for the viell-ascertained grievances of the sister country. Recognizing the failure el-the Land Aet of 1870, ~to aecomplish the objects it was intended to &thieve, and -the special requirements of Ireland in giving to the people a;proprietary interest irt the land; a measure will be, sub- Mined to this House to give m the Irish ' tenant farmer, (1) Cbmplete security under proper conditions in his bolding. (2) A marketable interest in his lane: (3) Exemption from 'exorbitant rent, and (4) facilities' te acquire a proprietary- Interest in the land he cultivates... You will also be asked to consider a measure to extend the municipal franchise in Ireland, in order to place it on the same basis as the fran- Chia in England., The subject of land reform in Engler]. has-also occupied- the attention of the Ministry, and Bills' for amending the law of property and facilitating disposi- tions of settled estates, and for simplifying and improving the -practice of conveyancing and making better prOvisiOn tespecting the remuneration of solicitors in conveyancing and other business will shortly be laid before-you. Yon will also be asked to consider whether the time has not new arrived for the assimilation of the Borough and -County Franchise. A•Bill for effectually repressing corrupt prac. tices, and linking paid. canvassing illegal, and for the ex-, tension of the hours of polling. and rendering the cloeing, of public houses during those hours imperative, will be•imme-' diately introduced. The Government propose to bring in Bills having for their objects respectively—the making illegal all dealings for profit with advowsons, or next presentations,, in the Church of England; the better regulation of works, Producing noxious gases—the repeal of all powers under., which licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquors to he con-, sumed off the premisee(commonly called" grocers' licenses,"), are at present granted or renewed, and the lend of licensed persons from the most oppressive special legislation and. taxation to whieh they are subject. The Government, if opportunity permits, will also introduce Bills to abolish actions for breach of promise of marriage; and to legalise marriage with a •deceased wife's sister. The subject of Indian Finance will receive the earnest consideration of the 'Government. The Government congratulate the House upon the signs of returning prosperity in trade, and they assure the House that they will at all times endeavour to , promote the commeroial interests of the country. In .cono I•clusion, the House may rely upon the Government preserv- ing the Constitution intact—upholding the connection between Church and State—and maintaining the dignity r- and prestige of the country abroad. 11 The following is a list of the Conservative Ministry:— First Lord of the Treasury, member for Montgomery, Mr, Massey; Chancellor of the Exchequer, member for Liver-. pool, Mr. Dee; Secretary of -state for Home Department. , member for Christchurch, Mr. J. 0. Drunciutnrass.—lsabella Milliams an elderlrlsronnan, having no fixed residence, Was fined is,. and testa afor, rbeing drunk, in a ,public-house, at Parra—JohtaLawretalion, a young man, residing in Eccleston, was charged-with being , drunk and disorderly, on Satnrday evening; be was further charged with committing.a breach of theapeace by fighting with 4 Man named Stirrup. P.C. Sherrift said lin refereed°. to the •latter charge that prisoner and twelve others were fighting previotia to their retiring to- the Militia Barracks This case was withdtawn, and defendant writ fined ssaitudi , coats for being drunk.—Thernais .Neil, Rainhill, waa,fined' ss. and costa, for being drankand'disOrderly, in thcbElough. Inna; DukeLstreet. ' . a- br, , CiErrnlG COIL OUT OF AN ! EMEANBMILTT. aarMary 'Callaghan and John O'Keeffe, Eccleston, were charged, with- maliciously damaging a railway embankment, belonging to the Greengate Colliery.—The wommi pleaded guilty, and the man saici he was there, .bilt te did no damage.--Mr. -ift, -who appeared to prosecute; said • the .people wtait to - it embankment, end. becauselthey found in it some Mlle aerial suitable :for; burning, they were in the habit of I ailing the embankment. to piece6.—P.C..lfossack, eta- , iioned at Greenbank Alkali Company, said he saw the male prisober,:whomte had 'cautioned many times, taking bits of inferior coal out of the embankment. He had ,a bag about three parts full;-which he left, on seeing thenfficear and ran away. Witheas followed bins, and asked his name, but he refused to give it. . He -Bad cautioned . him several., times. previously.—They were each fined 23. 6d. and costs, and Idi damage, being altogether 10s. Id. each. . eOLLISRS ASSAULTING * THE POLICE: HEATY FINE.—.- John Roberts and William. Robeita, young colliers, residing,' at Sutton, -were charged with being drunk and disorderly, in the highway, on Saturday night ; and also. with assaulting P.S. Batiks, whilst in the executioa At his duty.—P.S. Bankes said that on Saturday night the tato prisoners, with several others, all colliers, were cursing, shouting, and sing- , ing, at Wotsley Brow. He told them to go away' like good I fellows," but. they would - not, and said they had as , much right on the highway as the police. Witness told them if they persisted in going on in the manner they were doing that he would be obliged to report them. They then followed witness, Byrom shouting "Art ta going to do it, or not ?" meaning was he going,to report them. Witness told then to go away, and went towards Sutton, where he knew ' P.C. Denson would be. The two prisoners, with several . others, followed him shouting "Boycott him; kill him." Witness ordered P.C. Denson to take Byrom into custody, and he dklno. Byrom became rough and struck witness, and kicked him several times. Pieces of slag" were thrown about, and a general row commenced. Witness was so severely stunned that he was taken into a house close by in antate of insensibility.—P.C. Denson corroborated the latter portion of the above statement, anitstated that he saw the two prisoners kick Sergeant Banks.—Henry Whalley also gave-corroborative evidence, and said he went to the as- ' sistance of the police and took .Sergeant Banks into ids house and dressed his head.— James Lucas and Emilia 1 Whittaker gave evidence, of a confirmatory nature.—The Bench.said the charges of drunkenness would be withdrawn. The case was a very bad one indeed. They would each be fined £5 and oasts, or two moriths' imprisonment. A HUSBAND CHARGED WITH ' CRUELTY.:—James Spell- man. a caustic finisher, at Lockwood ana Leith, and residing in Wilson-street, between 30 and 40 years of. age, was charged with . assaulting -Margaret Spell- , man, his wife on Saturday night week.—Mr. swift said he appeared on the part of the wife, and if their wor- ships were satisfied that her future safety was in peril, asshe said it was, they had power to decree a jndicial separation, and order the husband to contribute bathe eupport.of his , wife and children.—Complainant saidehe and her husband had been married about twelve years; and had been living recently with a Mr; and Mrs. Naylahin Wilson-street. ;Her husband had been in bed most at the . week, but got up on. Saturday evening, soon after the had,gotte oot to do some business. About flare minutes to twelve be returned the worse for drink. She asked him what he would bave to his supper, , and said it was a nice thing to go out and come back at that I time at night in such a state after being tinder the doctor. I lie then made remarks about her character, saying that shel -was-worse than a certain bad woman; whereupon she left him with a candle, and took a lamp upstairs to make the bed. .He followed her up and asked lie what.sbe meant, and hit her on the face, knocking her upon the bed. She screamed •loudly, and he knocked her off the bed on to the floor. He then got his legs across her and commenced "thumping " her in almost every part of her body, and-continued to do so until Mrs. Naylor and her husband came to her assistance. Having got downstairs he" picked" her into the street, and ever since she had bad to keep out of his way as much as pos- sible. He had assaulted her repeatedly before, and she had had a child born with its shoulder knocked out, another with marks upon its face, while another was stillborn—the result of her husband's ill-treatment.—Mrs. Naylor said defendant was some times kind and some times cruel, but she grumbled a great deal, and he could not stand it. She had known him I to strike his wife many a time.—Defendant said that his , wife had been carrying on in a strange fashion while be was ill in bed. She had been jumping up and down the room.— Defendant called P.C. Sherriff, who said that complainant used very bad language about her husband when he called at the house with defendant's summons.—The Bench made an order of separation, the husband to pay 12s. a week for his wife and child's support..—Defendant asked if he was to have the furniture, and was answered in the affirmative. A DISCOVERY BY LOVERS.—John Parr a young man, re- , siding at Windle, was charged with being in an enclosed j backyard for an unlawful purpose, namely, stealing, on ' Saturday night.—A young woman named Alice Heashall, 19, Hamer-street, said that at nine o'clock on the evening in question she placed a board against the " bole " of the hencote, and reared some bricks against the board. In half an hour the board was down.—Thomas Houghton said he was in the yard on Saturday night with Annie Henshall sister to last witness, when he heard a noise, and almost simultaneously he heard the hens shout. He saw Parr step back from the hen place and run along by some boards.l Someone threw a stone which caudat him (witness) on the foot. The night was light and he recognised the prisoner: whom he had known eleven years.—Annie Henstall said ,she And Houghton were standing in the yard when the circum- stances as related by last witness took place. Parr had , previously lived with them for two years, and she was sorryl when ehe-found that it was prisoner who was in the yard.— Mr. Swift (who appeared for prisoner); Where was he when you saw him.? Running along by the boardsto get out of the yard. I suppose you and Houghton were courting in this yard.? Yes, sir (laughter a—Some body tias watching , on, I suppose. ? We were standing in the yard, and we beard ; a noise.—Didn't you see Mrs. Parr on Sunday morning after 1 her son bad been locked up.? Yes, sir.--Weli now didn't you All his mother that you wouldn't have sent tor the police, if you had known it was their Jack.? No, sir; I said I was very I sorry it was him as I had knowp him along time.—But you I didn't see him doing anything.?. No, sir.—P.C. Peebles 'apprehended prisoner in Lowe-street, carry log home some i beer for supper, and he charged him. He replied "I have I been in the house asleep for the last two hours," but he after'l wards said "1 have only come home to my supper."—Mal Swift submitted ithere was 'no felonious intention shown, against the prisoners and another thiadhe avaa not lawfully' in,custody. The information was laid under the Vagrancy , 'Aet, and they could not commit a person hy.warrant without a fresh pursuit, and it was not legal to adjudicate upon him.. But apart from that he submitted there was no case. Perhaps' he was going to court the other girl. (Laughter). The prisoner was discharged. , A YOUNG Tama—Frederick Liversedge, 14 yeara of age, was ,charged with stealing a vest, the property of John Callaghan.—A boy named Charles Gordon.' stated that on Saturday the prisoner met hint, in the Market-place, and 'offered him a vest for sale.. The prisoner agreed to take three halfpence for -it, and went with him into Victoria Passage to try it on.—P.C. Caunce said he saw the prisoner and Gordon In the passage with the vest, and on asking them where they had 'got it, thirpriSoner replied that be, had bought it from a Woman at a stall which be pointed out. He asked the woman about .it, and she stated that the prisoner had bought a pair of trousers from her during the days but not 'a , vest. "The prisoner thennaid he had takefl. it- from Callaghan's stall.---John: Callaghan identified the vent, and asked for his expenses for attending court, hirvino had to come from Manchester, and lose the market there.--a, ' Major Pilkingtonttoldhim that if it was,not for the proteca; t'airn of • the' policb everything ,es f his:etalamighl 14 ,slf:',ltns and therefore:had/lid no right to ask.for.exPenses, esPealaillt after the unsatisfactory and hesitating manner he had given his evidence,—The prisoner was ordered six strokes with a birch rod.
