div.p: __- LECTURE AT WIDNES ON FINANCIAL REFORM. Mr. John Noble, of London, de- On Tuesday evening, livered an interesting lecture on "Taxation, Local, and Imperial," under the auspices of the Financial Reform Association, in the Public Hall, Hutchinson-street, Widnes. There was a fair audience. Mr. Eustace Carey presided, in the absence Mr. E. K. Muspratt, president of the Widnes Liberal Association, and there were also upon the platform, Messrs. Martin Taylor, R. Holden Davis, and H. B. Shores, secretary to the Widnes Liberal Association. The CILAIRMAN said he had to apologise to them for his appearance in that position that evening; but he would read them a letter which would explain the situation. Mr. Mus- pratt, who was the president of the Financial Reform Asso- ciation had written to him that day, asking him to kindly take the chair that evening at Mr. Noble's lecture, and ex- press to the meeting his regret at being unable to attend, owing to his indisposition. The Widnes people had already had an opportunity of appreciating Mr. Noble's ability as a lecturer; and he was sure that he would be successful in making what was rather a dull subject both interesting and instructive. When the people learned how their mosey went, there would arise a strong movement for a retrench- mentw in our expenditure and remission of the taxes, ) He M hic h were a hindrance to trade and commerce. (Applause need not say how much he regretted Mr.uspatt'sabsence. M They, however, all knew how Mr. usprattrdid not spare himself in the work of forwarding any reforms—whether financial or otherwise; and they might rest assured that he would have been there that night 'if it havderbenienuephosfsni,ibilse.. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Muspratt was, however, y ceo dp—e aasnudr e woaf s buetatrei nig Posed—suffering from a very bait unable to attend. They had had th r Yr. Noble on previous occasions; and it would, therefore, be unnecessary for him to introduce him to them. The subject on which that gentleman had come to speak that night was, as they were all aware, financial reform. They all agreed that such reform was very necessary both in their local as well as their imperial affairs. (Applause.) Extrava- gant expenditure and good management were, in his opinion, contradictory terms; and it was impossible to have good management or efficiency without a true economy. Of course by economy he did not mean anything in the way of parsimony. (Hear, hear.) If he wanted a good pair of shoes, he did not go to a man and ask him to make them one as cheaply as possible—that was of brown paper—but he asked the workman to give him good value for his money. i So it was in imperial and local affairs. For his own part, , he believed that the English people would never be unwil- I ling to give a fair price for a fair article. (Hear, hear, and applause.) It was wonderful bow a good system of finance was at the foundation of almost every enterprise in life. That night the lecturer would give them his views upon how they might carry out local and imperial taxation with the least possible expenditure. Mr. NOBLE, who was received with loud applause, said they were met that night to consider a very important question one which came home to every one of them in that room, and especially to all the working men; because it depended, to a very large extent, upon the amount they had to pay in taxation, and upon the mode in which that taxation was levied, whether they should be able to pur- chase more or less of the conveniences and comforts of life with the wages they earned. Taxa- tion was generally considered to be rather a dry subject for a lecture ; but, notwithstanding that, it was one which interested them all; and it was there- fore, one into which every man should be anxious to en- quire. Their chairman had spoken to them upon the importance of finance. They saw every year, and almost every day, that those concerns whose financial affairs were wisely administered, where economy was practised, in which there was the least possible waste and the greatest possible value obtained for their money, were the concerns which prospered ; whilst, on the other hand, those which were ex- travagantly managed, and where there was no thrift, pru- dence, or forethought, were firms which would speedily come to grief, and intheir downfall throw out of employment vast numbers of the population. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Well, there was something analagous to this in the finan- cial concerns of nations and states; and they would gener- ally find that those governments which exercised economy, those which sought to get the greatest value for the money they expended, and by a sound system of finance to levy the taxation in the least oppressive mode, were those which conferred the greatest benefit and advantage upon the masses of the people. Many years ago they had in this country a very bad system of taxation indeed. It was a system which prevented the growth and expansion of trade; —a system which by imposing taxes upon every article that was bought, sold, manufactured, or used, restricted the employment of the masses of the population, and was one great cause of the pauperism and crime then found in the land. They had, happily, reformed that system, to a very large extent. Many hundreds of taxes that were formerly levied had been struck off the shoulders of the people. Forty or fifty years ago they had in their customs tariff about 1,200 articles and numerous duties of excise upon every- thing consumed by the working classes. Take the case of a man who was a buyer, and who had a wife and family. Everything that they wore in those days was taxed, from the hat or bonnet on the head down to the shoes and boots upon their feet ;—there was not a single article of clothing 'which had not paid its quota to the tax collector. Every article of food which came from abroad was also fully taxed, not so much for the purpose of raising a revenue for the State as of putting a good revenue into the pockets of the landlords. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The pretext made for this course of procedure was to tax the agricultural interest, but the real motive was to keep up war rents in time of peace. (Applause.) In 1840 they were not allowed to have from abroad any fresh meat— either beef, mutton or pork—neither were they allowed to import a single animal to be used as food. This plan was devised in the interest of the farmer. An almost prohibitive duty was placed upon bacon, hams, cheese and butter ; in short, there was no article that appeared upon the tables of the people but which, if it were purchased from abroad, had to contribute a heavy tax to the Government. Two articles were, however, admitted free, and it might be supposed that they were things necessary for the sustenance of the great mass of the population; but he was sorry to say it was no such thing. The two things which came in duty free were turbot for the rich man's table, and lobster to make the sauce with which to eat it! (Laughter and applause.) There were taxes upon the houses in which they lived—a tax upon the timber, a tax upon the tiles with which they were roofed, and a tax upon the windows. Indeed the taxes did not end there in the case of a man's house, for the very light of heaven was taxed as it came through the windows, if there were more than a certain number of them. (Applause.) All their furniture was taxed, and the very books they put upon their shelves—it the working people had books in those days --(A. Voice: "Aye !" and laughter]—Were also taxed; and when a prudent man, wishing to guard himself against loss , in the event of fire, went to the insurance office to insure ' his household goods, he had 3s. to pay to the Government sea tax upon the premium. They might suppose that by ' that . time matters had reached their climax, and so they had, for this multiplicity of taxes produced bad trade, scarcity of employment, and great distress amongst the population. The taxing, however, did not even end with their Louses and their furniture, for if they wished to make themselves clean by means of washing themselves, they could only do it by using taxed soap. In the good old days of Tory govern- ment their soap was taxed, and then they called the work- ing classes " the great unwashed." (Laughter.) The Tory party taxed their newspapers and books, and then told them they were too ignorant to have the franchise. All that had been changed, and with the most marked result as regarded the revenue of the country. Forty years ago £50,000,000 were collected from the people with great difficulty and trouble, whilst now the revenue was about £80,000.000, , which was collected with far less difficulty and pressure ' than the £50,000,000 forty years ago/ People often made mistakes as to the total amount of our taxation by incleding many wrong items in the estimate they made, such as, for instance, the rental of the crown lands, the surplus revenue from the working of the post-office and the telegraphs, which was not a tax, but the profit of commercial under- takings carried on by the Government. Then there was the large item of miscellaneous receipts, consisting largely of repayments advanced for services by the Government. Striking out all these, they found by a Parliamentary return that during the last financial year there had been taken from the people in the shape of taxes no less a sum than £68,000,000. They next came to the local taxation, in which there was the same thing to be observed as in the imperial. In the returns relating to this class of taxation several items were included which were not taxes. There was, for example, the money received for gas and water, when the sale of these two things was really in the hands of the local authorities. The payment for water was payment for a commodity, and was no more a tax than the money which a man paid for the beer he drank or the coal he burned. Dock dues and other such matters, which could not be described as taxes, were included, though not so. Striking out these they arrived at £21,090,000 as the stun paid in local rates, and £600,000 mainly levied in London in respect to the coal and wine duties, by indirect taxation; so that the total of their taxation, imperial and local, might be taken at £89,600,000. But this was not all, for there were taxes and taxes. There were taxes which took from the people just !e•ruch as was required by the governing authority; and lb,!cwere those which took a great deal more out of the pockets of the people than the sum needed by the governing.authorities. They might divide the taxes Into twodeszirtlons—direct and indirect. People did not like to pay taxes—they grumbled a great deal when they were called upon to put down ready money; but it seemed to him that was was s the wiser truest method of taxation twoiesnabplleaenv. every He rnbaeuliefvuelxdntohtve what he paid and when he paid when he would begin to ask "What am I paying it Lari taxation was extracted from themw(AwpipthlaouustetleiSr when they paid it, so long the o knowinglong as would have an extrava- gant expenditure—an expenditure their control. Of their imperial taxation some £45,000,000 would be beyond WAS now levied by means of duties of callus and excise. The great difference between those duties and a direct tax was this, that when the tax collector came to them for their local rates, every halfpenny so they paid, except some it tmall CoMmission, was received by the local authority; b w not so with the customs and excise. In the case of the lai latter, they paid a great deal more than the Government got; and be did not think there was any economy in the process. A great many difficulties had been made as to what the extra price was which they paid for their taxes in consequence of paying indirectly. He had been looking into this subject for years, and he did not believe ft was any lees than 50 per Cent. For every shilling the Government

got, they paid is. 6d., though he knew that some people thought it was only 25 per cent., or one fourth. Now he could give it them both ways. If it was 25 per cent. that they paid, it meant this, that on the £45,000,000 of taxation they paid £11,500,000 extra every year ; or if it was ,000,000 every year extra beyond sthoep£4er 57000nt.:000the they paid lht2h3e Government took. Now such things as those mounted up. In the one case it made the total taxation £101,000,000, and in the other above £112,000,000. Be did not think he was beyond the mark in this estimate, as one of the most successful members of the the present Government, Mr. Fawcett, the Postmaster- General, stated in a recent speech that every shilling paid in imperial taxation cost the taxpayer is. 3d. If they could only See the actual money they paid in taxes, instead of having it concealed from them, they would be perfectly astonished. They bought some beer, spirits, or coffee, and thought what they paid was the price of the article, but it was no such thing, as they paid for the article and the tax as well. They paid the profit upon the article and upon the tax, and that profit was a serious aggravation of the burden and the means whereby the whole burden of the State was thrown more largely than was just upon the shoulders of labour, whilst property was relieved to a like extent. What was the cause of all this? It was the con- sequence of past wars, for if peace could have been pre- served, there need to have been no occasion whatever for our huge national debt; there would need to have been very few taxes, and the whole of the populations of Europe might have been living together in a state of happiness and pros- perity, and this earth would have been an elvsium in com- parison with what it had been made into by the ambition of kings and so-called statesmen—(applause)ho had very rarely indeed seen the true interests of any of the people they had governed, but had constantly , been heaping excessive burdens upon the shoul- ders of their subjects, whilst they them- selves had been in pursuit of the veriest phantom which might have benefited a small fraction of the popula- tion, but which had been of no advantage whatever to the great mass of the people they had to govern. (Applause.) When they looked at the history of taxation in this country, especially in connection with the landed interest, there was unfolded a tale which must come home to everyone who studied it. They knew that for centuries the land in this country was held on condition that the holders of it should ' find soldiers for the King's wars. The lecturer briefly sketched the manner in which the greatlandowners managed to evade this responsibility on this acceunt, since which time the main burden of defending the realm had not fallen upon those who enjoyed a menoply of the soil but upon the mass of the people. Considerably more than half the soil of the country was held by 2,184 persons. These people, whilst enjoying all their old rights, had abandoned the obli- gation under which they first got the land into their posses- sion. It was time that this question should be looked into. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Having spoken of the manner in which the owners of real property for 150 years had bur- dened industry with heavy taxes, resulting in the trade of the country being very limited, the increase of wealth very slow, and the rise in the rental of the landed proprie- tors comparatively small, Mr. Noble said that during the last 40 years they had seen a great and marvellous change. They had seen restriction after restriction imposed upon industry in the shape of bad taxation, removed the com- merce, and the labour of the kingdom released from every burden in which it was swathed like a corpse in grave clothes. (Applause.) With that increase there bad been a vast advance in the rental of landed proprietors, and a great deal of that had been in what the late John Stuart Mill called the unearned increment of rent. Mill, in his "Ele- ments of Political Economy," asked upon what principle of justice had the landlord the right to all that increase in the value of his property, and argued at some length in favour of a special tex upon that "unearned increment" which the landlord had done nothing to produce, but which was the result of the improved state of the community generally, and in which the State ought unquestionably to share. (Applause.) But the landlords had done worse than that. When Pitt wanted money for his wars he put a probate duty upon personal property, intending at the same time to levy a tax upon real. The probate duty had stood upon personal property ever since, but it had never been put upon landed property. If a tradesman saved a few thousand pounds, which might be invested in extending his business, or in shares, and he died, leaving that property to his children, they could not receive one penny of it without first paying probate duty; but the largest estates, the most valuable properties of the great landed proprietors passed from father to son, or to the next heir, and not one penny was levied upon that in probate duty! (Applause.) Then there was the legacy duty which was first levied in the time of the long French war, and down to the year 1853, it had to be paid upon personal property, whilst real property was en- tirely free! Having spoken of Mr. Gladstone's legislation on the succession duty, Mr. Noble said even it was not a full measure of justice, as it was valued only on the life interest of the person succeeding to the property, so that he had to pay much less than if it were personal property. Take again the income tix. Was it just that the temporary and precarious earnings of the man of business, or of the clerk, which ceased with his life, and might stop before then if he was disabled by illness, should be taxed at the same rate as an income from real property, which the health of the holder did not at all effect, hut which remained, even after his death, for the benefit of his children and his family? (Ap.e plause.) These were matters which required the attention of the people, but he hardly expected to see them dealt with until they had secured an extension of the franchise to the people in the counties. Out of every pound sterling which they paid in taxes, 165. 10d. went either for past wars or the cost of preparation for future wars. Fancy Ifs. 10d. for wars and 3s, 2d. for all other purposes of Government; so that if they could only keep their rulers out of war the 3s. 2d. would suffice in every case were they now paid one pound. (Applause.) The lecturer next dwelt upon the great expansion of the tea trade which had taken place in India, and urged that our import duties upon that tea ou% t to be abolished so that the cotton duties might also be done away, and our trade with our Indian Empire receive a vast impetus. Mr. Noble next touched upon the questions of pensions and superannuations. He did not believe in either the one or the other, but considered that a man ought to be properly paid for his work, and then he ought to make his own pro- vision for the future. (Applause.) The Financial Reform Association had for years been preaching economy to the I people, but their action appeared to be almost "like a voice crying in the wilderness.' (Laughter.) Next followed an i eulogistic reference to the return of the master of fistance— Mr. Gladstone—to office, and the feeling of relief which was I then experienced by the whole country. Their present Chancellor of the Exchequer had removed the malt tax , which the Conservatives had dangled before the eyes of the, farmers for fifty years. (Applause and laughter.) He be. lieved that they might expect to see several important financial reforms carried out by Mr. Gladstone before he gave up office. It was because he (the speaker) thought he could discern in the fnture budget remissions of taxation which now oppressed the people of the country, that he hoped they would make their voices heard, and speak out in favour of an adjustment of taxation, so as to make property bear its fair share of the public burdens. The Tory Govern- ment was now gone; and they could only hope that the difficulties in which they involved us might now be solved as soon as possible, so that the country might withdraw from untenable positions—not by committing aggressions upon others—but that they might again firmly resolve to uphold, as they upheld fifty years ago, the great policy of peace, retrenchment, and reform. (Applause.) What they required was peace with all the world • a peace founded upon honour, because founded upon righteousness; a re- trenchment which should diminish the burdens of the people, and render their taxation lighter than it was at present; and a reform which should give them greater power in the administration of their own affairs, which should relieve the finances of the country, and seek to place them upon upon a more sound basis than that upon which they existed at the present time. (Loud applause.) Mr. MARTIN TAYLOR moved a vote of thanks to the lecturer, and said that they in Widnes were very much interested in a reduction of the Indian cotton duties, as chemicals were used so extensively in making these goods. He, therefore, hoped that they would do their best in every way to carry out such a desirable object. Take the case of of the United States. Before a ton of caustic soda went into that country the purchaser must pay £l3 per ton in the way of duty. They could easily understand that with such a duty upon caustic soda, the sale of it was materially decreased. He hoped they would carefully ponder the very interesting facts placed before them by Mr. Noble. Mr. DAVIS, in seconding the miaion, which was carried with enthusiasm, said the lecture had fairly bristled with points. A similar compliment was paid to the Chairman, on the proposition of Mr. NOBLE, seconded by Mr. SHORES, and the proceedings terminated.

MEETING OF COLLIERS' WIVES AT FARNWORTH. THREATENING TO SHOOT THE MASTERS. A meeting of the wives of the colliers on strike was held on Tuesday in the Farnworth Market Place. The bellman had not been able to get over the district he was commis- sioned to visit before the women began to gather in large numbers. Out of curiosity about 1,000 men assembled to watch the proceedings. The chair wasl occupied by a Stal- wart amazon familiarly known as "Nan" Norris. She said she would rather stop out until " Kesmas " than go in at the present rate of wages. She got her living by washing, and if she were a collier she would take in washing rather than go down the pit for the paltry sum they got. (Hear, hear, and cheers.)—A Mrs. Mason said her husband was I always grumbling when he came home, and it was no won. der, for there was so little for anybody to eat.—Anothe?" woman said they wanted neither police nor soldiers to look after them. Let seven policemen go and eat nine pounds of ham and call for more, as they had done; let them mind their own affairs, and the miners could look after theirs.—A virago said if anyone would give her a gun and a cap she would shoot the masters. If they were all of the same mind as her, they would go to Worsley and not leave a brick on the hall. (A voice: 'There's plenty of the same mind," and laughter.) Well, those of that mind hold up their hands. (A number of hands were then held up.)— Mrs. Rogers said she would do the same as other women had offered to do, if anyone would give her a gun.—At the con- clusion of the meeting a procession was formed, and walked off to Walkden to see Mr. Clifford Smith, manager to the Trustees. The courage of the processionists seemed to evaporate as they proceeded to the offices, and the host • vanished gradually along the route. Only about 20 perse- vered to the end of the pilgrimage.

(Hear, hear.) Well, they knew ignorance and sin were the parents of poverty, and every year nearly £10,000,000 were spent in relief of the poor. That was not the account which was paid in the form that they called poor rates, but the amount actually paid either in out-door relief or in connection with their workhouses. The figures he had quoted gave them a sad account of the state of this Christian country. (Hear, hear.) Something had been done to try to elevate the masses ; and he really thought it was the most difficult problem with which all who took an in- terest in the welfare of those around them had to deal. Much had been done during a considerable period now, but more especially during later yea:s, in connection with sani- tary matters, with the improvement of dwellings for the working classes; and they knew that these things were very important indeed,if they hoped to improve the position of the masses of the people in our large towns and cities, and in our villages. Of late years a very great deal more had been done than was formerly the case in connection with education. The Government grant for education was last year nearly £3,500,000 in aid of the day schools which were established throughout the length and breadth of the country. Of course they knew that in addition to this amount which was granted by Government, vast sums were raised by voluntary contributions, and spent in the educa- tion of the people. A vast amount of work was carried out now-a-days in connection with their temperance societies. They brought the influence of these to bear upon the masses of the people, so far as they could get at them, so that in connection with sanitary improvements, with imp oved dwellings, with education, and with the propagation of the principles of temperance, a great deal had been done far the masses of the people; but they must never forget that how- ever much was carried out in these ways, unless they took the gospel to them, it was all in vain. It was right for them to try to raise the people as regarded their physical state; it was right for them to do all that they could to elevate them intellec- tually, but they must take the Gospel to them, and save their souls, if it were possible to do so. (Hear, hear.) They must not, however, forget that each one of them had a duty towards their poor brothers and sisters throughout the length and breadth of the land, with regard to the saving of their souls, from which they could not free themselves, and unless they did what they could in this respect, they would net be free from great blame. For many years past their home mission work had been increasing, and doing a great amount of good; and he thought that if they knew more about the state of the poor people around them; if they knew more of the importance of the missions which were being used and would be used to a vastly greater extent if they would only find the money to do it with, they would feel more and lee inclined to do more than they had done in this direction. (Applause.) The Rev. J. H. Monosx, of Liverpool, who attended as one of the deputation, delivered a speech characterised by I much enthusiasm and spiritual feeling. Ile dwelt upon the I importance of the Wesleyans of this age not forgetting the place from which they were hewn, and the fact that the denomination at the first part of its history devoted itself almost exclusively to what might be described as home mis- sion work. He was afraid that some of their members were ' inclined to say that they had now become matronly, and they could not think of doing work which was more fit for youg men and enthusiasts generally ;—they left that sort of labour to the Primitive Methodist denomina- tion and the Salvation Army. (Laughter and applause.) They were inclined to say "I am a lady of kingdoms now; I have sonorous organs now; I have splendid choirs now, and you vile people must not touch me !" Let Methodism yield to that fascinating address and sentiment, and her days would soon be numbered; Ichabod would come out in letters of fire upon her palaces, and her glory would go down in the dust. Let the prim' precise preacher who thought almost as much of the shape of a sentence as the saving of a soul, preach in the mission rooms, and his spirit would soon come nearer to that of the Master. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. J. S. PAWLTN, of London, who attended as the second member of the deputation, regretted to say that there were some members of the denomination whose zeal in spiritual work was just in inverse proportion to that which they manifested in worldly matters. They were swift as the gazelle in the race for worldly position and success, but slow as the tortoise in spiritual • matters. He was thoroughly convinced that if the people belonging to the denomination did their duty, there was not one of their chapels which they could not fill to the very doors. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The proceedings terminated shortly afterwards.

DAMAGES FOR REPUDIATION OF CONTRACT. At the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Stephen and a special jury.— Wait v. Whitaker and others.—ln this casa Mr. Gully, Q.C., and Mr. Kennedy, instructed by Messrs. Jeans and Morgan, of Manchester, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Russell, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Collins, instructed by Messrs. Eastwood, of Todmorden, appeared for the defen- dants. The action was brought to recover damages for loss sustained through repudiation of contract. It appeared that the plaintiff, Edward James Wait, was a manufacturer of china day, having works in Cornwall; and the defendants, Edward Whitaker and Sons, were warp sizers, , belonging to Todmorden. On the 19th June, 1879, a contract was entered into between the parties whereby the plaintiff was te supply the defendants with 500 tons of the best china clay at 38s. per ton, in quantities of 20 to 25 tons a week. Defendants on the 4th August, 1879, were given notice by the plaintiff that the clay was awaiting them at Runcorn. After various letters had been exchanged, the defendants repudiated the contract, although it was signed "Edward Whitaker, for Whitaker and Sons." As the clay, lying at Runcorn idle was incurring expense, the plaintiff was at , length compelled to dispose of it at 265. per ton, thus leaving a balance due to him on the contract price of £3OO, which he claimed. The defendants had paid £6O into court, and Mr. Collins, on their behalf, said that Edward Whitaker was practically liable—that he admitted the other two defen- dants, who were his trustees, were not liable. They were unaware of the existence of the contract until four or five months after it had been made.—His Lordship ruled that the trustees were liable, if only for nomftal damages, and the learned counsel then addressed the court in mitigation of damages.—The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff for the full amount claimed.

that he participated in the ballot; but when the ballot was over all who liked to become members had not to pay up the back subscriptions, but would have to pay four weeks if they got a ballot. The ballot took place, and they would assume that Smith got it. Smith got £lOO. With it he might buy property or select a site for building where he liked. He gave the particulars to the secretary, who got the surveyor to survey. In the rules they asked the sur- veyor to report to the Board of Trustees, and to give his practical opinion as to the commercial value of the property. They then asked the trustees to lend the commercial value without deductions. The permanent societies had a right to ask for a margin, because they had not only to secures the principal, but their interest as well. Their societies had no interest to secure, and therefore lent the full value to a , member who bought and often lived in the house. And if he had not got the small sum of £4 4s. for law charges they lent him it for twelve months. The member getting the ballot generally got it unexpectedly, and did not know what to do with it. In that case he returned it to the society until he was ready for it. It became re-ballotted,and another member got it. In six or twelve months time the first member found what he wanted, and gave notice to the secretary, and when the last ballot was made preceding the notice he got his money. There was another way. They might sell it if they pleased, and get for it £lO or £l2, although they had only paid 2s. The person who bought the ballot took the member's place in the society. This man found property where he liked, and had it surveyed and mortgaged as he had described. There was a choice of repayment. He might repay it at £8 or £lO a year; invariably it was eight, and in 12i years he paid the borrowed money. He paid his 6d. a week all the time, and this amounted to £l6 ss. lie con- tracted a debt of £27 65.,. and they now said to him, "You have got this property not with your £l6 ss.' but with the members' combined money, and now, instead of taking a long period at 6d. a week, we make you pay Xl.O neat year." After that they said to the member that he must lend his £27 6s. to the society until every member had had his turn. How long would it be before the last member got his ballot? They could tell that on being informed how many members would remain together. Assuming that none left out of the 500 who paid 6d. a week and repay- ments, they would without doubt get their ballot in 25 years. div.head: BREAM OF PROMISE OF MARRIAGE
div.p: CASE. At the Salford Hundred Court of Record, on Tuesday, before Mr. H. W. West, Q.C., Recorder, the case of Lee v. Summersall was heard. This was an action to assess damages for breach of promise of marriage. The plaintiff, Lucy Lee, is a widow, residing at Collinge-street, Heywood, and is employed at there as a weaver, and the defen- dant, Benjamin &immersell, is a loom-jobber residing at the same place. The plaintiff's case was that in consequence of overtures which the defendant made to her she frequently met him and ultimately he made her an offer of marriage, telling her that be was earning from £2 to £2 ss. per week. The plaintiff accepted the offer, and was ocknowledged by the defendant as his future wife. She had three children, two of whom were married,. one of them (a daughter) being married in January, Ind, in consequence of her mother's engagement to the defendant. A week before the marriage was to have taken place the defendant came to her and said that "he was not going on with it, as she owed so much money," the fact being that she owed scarcely any money at all. About a month after this, the defendant married another woman in better circumstances than the plaintiff. —ln defence the defendant said that at the time he made the promise be was not aware that the plaintiff was consider- ably in debt. After about two minutes' deliberation the jury returned a verdict for £5.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DEATH NEAR PRESTON BROOK.
div.p: On Thursday morning, about six o'clock, the body of a man was found dead on the railway, near Bridsvrood Junc- tion, by a man named John Speed, but the circumstances by which he met with his death are at present a mystery. He had been seen alive about an hour before that time, and, from his actions then, would appear to have been suffering under some delusion. He was running from the pursuit, be said, of "two men with two knives "that were going to kill him, and appeared to be much frightened. He was respec- tably dressed, but the body has not yet been identified, and he evidently does not belong to the district in which he was found. An inquest was held on the body at Dutton Work- house, on Friday, before Mr. Ridgway, the coroner. The first witness called was Thomas Roberts, labourer at Aston Heath, who deposed to seeing the deceased on Wednesday morning, the 10th instant, about five o'clock. He was walking from his cottage to his work when he saw the deceased, whom he did not know, running after him. Witness asked" Where are you of in such a hurry," and he replied "There are two men after me with two knives. They are going to kill me." Deceased said he had come from Ches- ter and had been" running all night." Witness asked if he had killed anyone. "They have a mind to say so" was the reply. The two then walked together for some distance, and on arriving at the house where witness was employed, the deceased ran into the yard before him and entered the building. Witness went into the stables to attend to the horses, and had been there about ten minutes when the de- ceased came in, closed tht door, and held the latch with both hands for some minutes. He then sat down on a stone trough in the stable. Witness went out to get " the Irish- men up," and when he returned the deceased had departed. He had missed a fork which he had been using. The de- ceased seemed " sadly frightened " when he met him. He thought deceased was an Englishman. Alfred Bennett, living attrewe, said he was an engine driver for the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany. He was driving the 5.5 train from Crewe to Liver- pool on Wednesday morning. The train left Crewe at 5-14, and when passing the signal box at Birdswood Junction, about 5-40, he felt something unusual, and the steam tap was shut off. He went forward to Warrington, and reported the case. lie thought it was something that had, fallen from another train. It was very dark. Joseph Henry Outram, of Tunnel Top, Dutton, said he was walking on the railway near Birdswood Jurction, when he saw something laid across the line, which he found to be the body of the deceased. He was laid with his head on the crossing, face downwards, and his body in the down four- foot of the Runcorn line. There was a bad cut on the left eye, and a small hole on the back of the head. The body iras quite warm. He found one of the boots of deceased about two yards from the body. P.C. Speed, stationed at Dutton. said the body of the deceased was that of a man about 5f t. 2in. high, having light brown hair and sandy moustache. He appeared to be about 35oir4t0vears of age. There were three or four teeth miss- ing n he front top jaw, and his hands were soft and white. He had on a black cloth coat and white moleskin trousers; black cloth cap, and elastic-side boots. All the clothes were in good condition, and clean. His shirt was a common check, and round his neck was a black and white check scarf. In the pockets be had, found two old pocket handker- chiefs, but there were no marks on any of the articles. He did not know deceased, and had been unable to trace him. The jury returned a verdict of "Found dead."

pURSUANT to an order of the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, made in an action in the matter of the estate of MARGARET KENWRIGHT, widow, deceased, SMITH against KENWRIGHT. The CREDITORS of MAR- GARET KENWRIGHT, late of Burtonwood, in the County of Lancaster, farmer, who died on or about the 9th day of October, 1874, are on or before the 26th day of February, 1881, to send by post, prepaid, to Robert Davies, of the firm of Robert Davies and Co., of Warrington, in the County of Lancaster, the solicitors of the Defendants, John Kenwright and Jonathan Hen wright, the executors of the will of the deceased, their christian and surnames, addresses and descriptions, the full par- ticulars of their claims, a statement of their accounts, and the nature of the securities (if any) held by them; or, in default thereof, they will be peremptorily excluded from the benefit of the said Order. Every Creditor holding any security, is to pro- duce the same before the Vice-Chancellor, Sir Charles Hall, at his Chambers. situated No. 14, Chancery-lane, Middlesex, on Monday, the 14th day of March, 1881, at 12 o'clock at noon, being the time appointed for adjudicating on the claims.— Dated this.27th day, of January, 1881. H. F. CHURCH, Chief Clerk. COLE AND JACKSON, 36, Essex-street, London, Agents fer ROBERT DAVIES & Co., Warrington.

MAKINSON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received, hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practical experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himself on a large scale; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWRIGHT busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice in Valuing and Selling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant. Growing and Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-in- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases Involving Damage and Trespass. Mr. WILCOCK, also, has had the advantage of being brought up to Farming, together with that of having served an appren- ticeship to an eminent Veterinary Surgeon, combined with the experience he has had since his connection with this firm, enables him to give judicious and valuable advice in all cases in which he may be consulted. In conclusion, H. and W. beg their friends and the public generally to note that they have a trustworthy and efficient staff of assistants in their employ, who have been carefully trained to watch over the interests of those who favour the firm with their patronage; whilst last, but not least, their system of advertising, and the facilities they possess of ensuring an extensive circulation, enable them to offer the utmost pos- sible publicity to any sales entrusted to their management.
